passages.text: This book explains the why behind your Levlofit plan. Read the opening chapters in order, then come back to any chapter when a question comes up.

Volume | What you will learn. Volume: I. Training; What you will learn: Starting safely, how your plan is built, how training works, technique, warming up, sessions, lighter weeks, plateaus and injury prevention. Volume: II. Nutrition; What you will learn: The basics, protein, vegetarian eating, calories, gaining weight, eating too little, timing, budget, supplements, water and eating out. Volume: III. Recovery; What you will learn: Sleep, stress, mobility, soreness, motivation, habits and daily steps. Volume: IV. Physique; What you will learn: Body fat, proportions, lagging muscles and posture. Volume: V. Tracking; What you will learn: Photos, measurements, body weight, your workout log, reviews and goals. Volume: VI. Disciplines; What you will learn: General fitness, strength, calisthenics, running, HYROX, boxing, kettlebells, home training, training as a woman and training after 40

Chapter overview. Each chapter opens with its main idea.. Evidence notes. These say how strong the research is. Foundations explains the grades.. Levlofit rules. A number Levlofit uses where research gives no exact figure. Treat it as a sensible starting point, not a research finding.. Source marks. Numbered marks point to the full list at the end of each chapter.. Key takeaways. Each chapter ends with a short summary.

Word | Meaning in this book. Word: Session; Meaning in this book: One training appointment, from warm-up to the last set. Word: Set and rep; Meaning in this book: A rep is one lift; a set is a group of reps done without rest. Word: RIR; Meaning in this book: Reps in reserve: how many more good reps you could have done. Word: Deload; Meaning in this book: A planned lighter week to shed fatigue. Word: Maintenance; Meaning in this book: Eating about as much energy as you burn. Word: Level; Meaning in this book: Your stage, 0 to 5, in each goal; levels are earned with a level check. Word: Protocol; Meaning in this book: The app screen where you change your goals, training days and diet. Word: Workout; Meaning in this book: The app tab with your sessions and level checks

This book is | This book is not. This book is: For healthy adults aged 18 and over; Levlofit plans cover ages 18 to 80; This book is not: Medical advice, or a replacement for your doctor, physiotherapist or dietitian. This book is: Built on cited guidelines and research, with numbers named to their source; This book is not: Written for children or teenagers, who have their own activity guidelines. This book is: A companion to your plan in the app; This book is not: A plan for pregnancy or a medical condition without your doctor's input
Evidence: strong. WHO gives separate physical activity recommendations for children and adolescents aged 5 to 17, so this adult book does not apply to them.
Start here. Read the next chapter, Safe to start. If any of its questions apply to you, see a doctor before you train.

The book has six volumes: Training, Nutrition, Recovery, Physique, Tracking and Disciplines.. Evidence notes say how strong the research is. Levlofit rules are starting points, not findings.. It is written for adults, and it does not replace your doctor.
Fitness looks complicated because there is so much advice. Results come from a short list of basics, done for a long time. Get these right before you worry about anything else.
5 · things · decide almost all of your results. 150 · min a week · of moderate activity, the health minimum. 2 · days a week · of strength training for every adult

What decides your results. Train hard enough · Sets that end a few reps short of failure, on a plan that suits your level.. Progress over time · Add reps, weight or sets as you get stronger, so the work keeps asking more of you.. Eat for your goal · The right calories for losing, keeping or gaining weight, and enough protein every day.. Recover · Sleep, rest days and lighter weeks: the body adapts between sessions, not during them.. Keep going · Months and years of the four above beat any perfect plan you stop after three weeks.

Everything else (exact exercises, meal timing, supplements, gadgets) changes results far less. Spending your energy on details while the basics slip is the most common way to stall. See Progressive overload and Nutrition fundamentals.

Exercise. For today: you feel good, you move, you burn energy.. Any activity on any day counts.. Great for health and mood.. Training. For a goal months away: a stronger lift, a faster run, a different body.. Each session builds on the last, so the plan matters.. Needs a proven programme, and progress you can measure.

Both are good. Levlofit builds a training plan, because that is how bodies change on purpose. If you only want to be active, any movement you enjoy, done most days, meets the health goal. See General fitness and heart health.
People who fail often try to change everything in one week. Pick one or two changes you are sure you can keep, and add more only when those feel easy.

A first month that sticks. Week 1 · Train on two fixed days. Keep sessions short. Add one glass of water each morning.. Week 2 · Same days. Add vegetables to one meal a day.. Week 3 · Add a third session if the first two felt easy. Start logging your sets.. Week 4 · Hit your protein target on most days. Weigh in once a week, same time of day.
Going to the gym once a week, every week, beats a perfect plan you drop. Habits grow from repetition, not motivation. See Building habits that last.

Realistic first-year changes. Muscle, men new to training · 0.9 · about 0.5 to 1 kg a month in the first year, then slower [per month]. Muscle, women new to training · 0.45 · about half of that [per month]. Fat loss, sustainable pace · 2.5 · 0.5 to 1% of body weight a week (about 2 to 3 kg a month for a 70 kg person) [per month]

These are rough planning figures from coaching experience, not promises; genetics, age, sleep and how well you eat all move them. Visible change usually needs 2 to 3 months. Muscle comes slower than most people expect; fat loss comes faster than muscle gain. Losing fat and gaining muscle at the same time is possible for beginners and people returning after a break, but slower than doing one at a time. See Losing and gaining weight: your questions.
Whatever you want, it breaks down into some mix of these:
Lose some fat.. Gain some muscle.. Strength training.. Cardio and conditioning.. Skill in particular movements (a pull-up, a run, a punch).. The eating that supports the above.
A "toned" look, for example, is some muscle plus low enough body fat to see it. A marathon is mostly cardio, some strength and a lot of skill practice. Name the mix and the plan becomes obvious.

Strength training gives you. Stronger bones and a lower risk of osteoporosis. Better balance and fewer falls as you age. Lower blood pressure and better blood sugar. Easier daily life: lifting, carrying, climbing stairs. It does not. Make you bulky by accident: building lots of muscle takes years of effort. Make you slow or inflexible when you train through a full range. Need a gym: bands, bodyweight and dumbbells work. Replace cardio; you want both
Cardio adds a stronger heart and lungs, better recovery between sets, mood and sleep. It does not "kill your gains". See Heart rate, sweat and calories burned.
Motivation comes and goes. Habits and a plan carry you on the days it does not show up.

Love the result, not every session. Many people never enjoy every workout; they enjoy being fitter.. Separate training and play. Train to your plan, and keep a sport or walk you do just for fun.. Keep goals quiet until you have done the work. Announcing a big goal can feel like progress already made, which makes people less likely to follow through. Share what you have done, not what you will do.. Expect bad weeks. Miss a day, return the next. One missed week changes nothing; quitting changes everything.

Training hard enough, progressing, eating for your goal, recovering and staying consistent decide almost everything.. Start with one or two changes you can keep, then build.. Muscle comes slowly; give any plan 2 to 3 months before judging it.. Strength training helps everyone, and cardio helps your lifting.
Most adults can start exercising today. A small group should speak to a doctor first, and everyone should know the few signs that mean stop.
Screening rests on three things: how active you are now, any signs or known disease, and how hard you plan to train. Go through these questions in order.

Question | If yes | If no. Question: Do you have chest pain, fainting, unusual breathlessness, a racing heartbeat or ankle swelling?; If yes: Stop here. See a doctor before exercising.; If no: Go to the next question.. Question: Has a doctor told you that you have heart, kidney or metabolic disease such as diabetes?; If yes: Get medical clearance first, then start light and build slowly.; If no: Go to the next question.. Question: Are you mostly inactive right now, exercising fewer than 3 days a week?; If yes: Start at light to moderate effort and build up over weeks.; If no: Carry on, and build intensity gradually.

Normal during training | Stop and get help. Normal during training: Muscles burning near the end of a set; Stop and get help: Chest pain, pressure or tightness. Normal during training: Breathing hard, then recovering within a minute or two; Stop and get help: Dizziness, faintness or confusion. Normal during training: Muscle soreness a day or two later; Stop and get help: A heartbeat that feels irregular or racing. Normal during training: ; Stop and get help: Sharp or sudden joint pain
Some activity is better than none, even if you cannot reach the target yet. If you have been inactive, start low and build slowly.
Follow your doctor's advice first. Pregnant, recovering from surgery, or managing a long-term condition? Follow your doctor's advice first. Levlofit will ask you and adjust.

Most adults can start today; some should see a doctor first.. Chest pain, fainting, dizziness or an irregular heartbeat mean stop and get help.. Some activity is better than none. Start low and build slowly.
Levlofit is built level first. You train your main goal until the basics are solid, then new goals unlock.

Level | Name | What it means. Level: 0; Name: Starting out; What it means: Learn the moves, build the habit.. Level: 1; Name: Foundation; What it means: Basic strength and fitness in place.. Level: 2; Name: Building; What it means: Steady progress on your main goal.. Level: 3; Name: Solid; What it means: A good level for most people.. Level: 4; Name: Advanced; What it means: Specialised training pays off.. Level: 5; Name: Expert; What it means: Coach-led territory.
You move up in four steps: train the plan, log your sets, take the level check, and unlock the next level.

How to read this chapter. This chapter is orientation, not science. It explains how the Handbook grades evidence and where its limits are. The science starts in Exercise science.

Fitness does not lack information. The information is unsorted. A careful review of many trials and a confident video reach you through the same feed, in the same format, with the same air of authority. Nothing tells you which claim rests on twenty trials and which rests on an explanation someone found plausible.

The result is rarely that people fail to train. They train for years while changing what they do, and never build enough uninterrupted progress in one direction to see a result. What is usually missing is not effort. It is a stable framework, and a way to tell strong claims from weak ones.
This Handbook aims to tell you what to do, and also how confident anyone should be that it works.
It is a reference covering training, nutrition, recovery, physique and tracking progress. Your Levlofit plan tells you what to do today. The Handbook explains why.

Property | What it means for you. Property: It explains; What it means for you: Recommendations come with their reasoning, so you can adapt them when your situation differs.. Property: It grades its confidence; What it means for you: Where the evidence is weak or divided, it says so instead of choosing a side to read better.. Property: It is made to be re-read; What it means for you: What is useful to you changes as you train for longer.
Claims carry one of six grades. These are the Handbook's own reading of the sources, not grades given by the papers.

Grade | What it means | Wording used. Grade: Strong; What it means: Several good reviews, or a current position stand from a recognised body.; Wording used: "Evidence shows". Grade: Moderate; What it means: Consistent findings with real limits.; Wording used: "Evidence suggests". Grade: Emerging; What it means: Early human evidence.; Wording used: "Early evidence indicates". Grade: Insufficient; What it means: No adequate human evidence either way.; Wording used: "Not established". Grade: Contested; What it means: Credible evidence on both sides.; Wording used: "Evidence is divided". Grade: Practical; What it means: Sensible guidance, or personal preference, that research has not settled.; Wording used: "In practice"

Two rules follow. An explanation of how something might work inside the body is not a result, and does not justify a recommendation by itself. And "not established" means the question is open, not that the answer is no.

A useful habit. When you meet a confident fitness claim, do not ask only whether it is true. Ask what someone would have had to measure to know it. Many popular claims fail that question straight away.
These are working defaults, not scientific findings.

Consistency beats intensity. The plan you follow for two years beats the better plan you follow for six weeks.. Technique defines the load. A repetition done differently is a different exercise, whatever the log says.. Recovery is part of training. It is an input to adaptation, not a reward for having trained.. Progress is measured in months. Change from week to week is mostly noise: water, sleep, food timing and measuring error.. Evidence first, then what you will keep doing. Where the evidence is absent, choose the option you will actually sustain.

One number makes a poor target. Body weight cannot separate muscle gained from food eaten, and a mirror cannot separate real change from better lighting. Track several things, because they move at different speeds and rarely all stall at once.

What to track | What good looks like | Rough timescale. What to track: Strength; What good looks like: More work at the same standard of technique, on the same exercises.; Rough timescale: Weeks. What to track: Physique; What good looks like: Balanced development, with body fat controlled rather than as low as possible.; Rough timescale: Months. What to track: Health; What good looks like: Fitness, joint comfort and everyday movement improving or holding.; Rough timescale: Months. What to track: Recovery; What good looks like: Handling more training than a year ago without building up fatigue.; Rough timescale: Months to years. What to track: Sustainability; What good looks like: Still training, still enjoying it, still free of injury, years later.; Rough timescale: Years
The last row decides the others.

Read this volume in order. The next few chapters give you the words every later chapter uses.. Use the rest as reference. Go to the chapter that answers the question you have now.. Check the grade before acting. A moderate claim deserves a trial in your training. An insufficient one deserves curiosity, not a change of plan.. Change one thing at a time. Two changes together give a result you cannot explain.. Re-read the basics. They become more useful as you train for longer.

What this Handbook is not. This is general information for healthy adults. It does not diagnose conditions, read medical or lab results, or give individual medical, psychological or clinical nutrition advice.. See a qualified health professional before starting or continuing if you have a diagnosed condition, are pregnant or have recently given birth, are managing an injury, have pain during exercise, or have a history of disordered eating. Nothing here should delay care you would otherwise seek.

Much of the research behind this Handbook studied young adults, more often men, over weeks to months. The further you are from that description, the more carefully you should apply it. Food examples are written for Indian kitchens and budgets. That shapes the examples, not the science.

The problem is unsorted information, not missing information.. Claims carry a visible grade. Check it before acting.. An explanation is not a result, and "not established" does not mean false.. Progress has several parts and is measured in months. Sustainability decides the rest.. This is education, not clinical care.
Training works because a signal, repeated often enough and recovered from well enough, changes your muscle. Exercise choice, sets, rest, food and sleep all exist to protect or strengthen that signal.
This chapter explains the signal and the few variables that control it. Read it once, then come back whenever a later recommendation seems arbitrary.

Adaptation is a change in your body that makes a hard demand easier. Lift a load your body is not yet equipped for, recover, and you become a little better equipped. Stop the demand and the change slowly reverses. That is also why a plan you have outgrown stops working even though nothing about it changed.

Adaptation | What changes | Roughly how fast. Adaptation: Nervous system; What changes: Better coordination and confidence under load. The muscle is not bigger yet.; Roughly how fast: Days to weeks. Adaptation: Muscle; What changes: Muscle fibres grow thicker.; Roughly how fast: Weeks to months. Adaptation: Connective tissue; What changes: Tendons and ligaments slowly adapt.; Roughly how fast: Months

These timescales are a teaching guide, not measured limits for you. The order still matters. Early strength gains come quickly and often before your body visibly changes, so do not expect the mirror to keep up with the bar in the first weeks.

The leading explanation for muscle growth is mechanical tension: the force a muscle fibre experiences as it works against resistance. Fibres that are recruited and work hard receive the signal to build.
The practical point is this: judge a set by whether its last repetitions were truly hard with acceptable technique. A set stopped far short of that is likely to do less.
In practice. "Feeling the muscle" and "getting a pump" are sensations. They do not tell you by themselves that a set will build muscle.
A common story says training damages muscle and the body repairs it bigger. The measurements do not support it as the main cause.

Evidence: moderate. In ten young men followed through ten weeks of training, muscle damage and protein synthesis were both highest in the first week, but neither was related to muscle growth. By weeks three and ten, damage had fallen and the rise in protein synthesis correlated strongly with growth (r about 0.9). This is one small study of mechanisms.
The authors conclude that growth comes from many small rises in protein synthesis, as damage fades. Two things follow in practice:

Soreness is not a score. A new exercise or a long break can leave you very sore. A well-run session months later can leave you less sore and still be useful.. Do not chase damage. Seeking soreness adds recovery cost, and that cost can come out of your next session.
Once tension is the signal, planning comes down to three questions: how much hard work, how often, and how hard.
Volume means hard working sets per muscle per week. It has the clearest link to growth.

Evidence: strong for more volume, moderate for the shape of the curve. The American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) position stand found that growth was enhanced by 10 or more sets per muscle group per week, with a dose-response.. A review of 67 studies found that size and strength both rise with volume, with diminishing returns that are much stronger for strength. Counting an assisting set as half a set predicted results best.

So more tends to give more, and each extra set buys less. The Handbook gives no personal target above 10 sets, because your recovery, history and stress decide what you can use. Count a set that trains a muscle directly as one, and a set where it assists as half. Rows train your biceps. Presses train your triceps.

With weekly volume equal, training a muscle more often did not change growth. It does appear to help strength: the ACSM found strength was enhanced by 2 or more sessions a week, and could not determine an upper limit.
In practice, frequency is mainly a way to deliver volume. Spreading many sets across more days can keep the later sets from fading.
Repetitions in reserve (RIR) is how many more repetitions you could have done with acceptable technique when you stopped. Two left is 2 RIR. No more possible is 0 RIR, called momentary failure.

Evidence: moderate that hard training is enough; insufficient that failure adds anything. A review of 15 studies found no advantage for growth from training to momentary failure over stopping short (effect size 0.12, confidence interval -0.13 to 0.37). A looser definition of failure gave a trivial advantage (0.19, 0.00 to 0.37). The authors suggest a possible non-linear relationship.. A later analysis found growth improved as sets ended closer to failure, while strength barely changed. Its authors call it exploratory, because the RIR values were estimated.. The ACSM reports that training to momentary fatigue did not consistently affect outcomes, and its main recommendation is to train with high effort.
These fit together if benefit grows as a set becomes truly hard, then flattens before failure. That is a hypothesis, not a proven curve.

Goal | Reasonable default | Why. Goal: Muscle; Reasonable default: About 1 to 3 repetitions left; Why: A practical default. Growth may suffer if you stop far short, and failure has not been shown to add more.. Goal: Strength; Reasonable default: 2 or more left; Why: Strength looks similar across a wide range.. Goal: Both; Reasonable default: Failure not required; Why: Not shown to be necessary for either.
Shorter rest makes training feel harder. That does not make it more productive.

Evidence: moderate for a small benefit past about a minute; insufficient that short rest harms growth. A review of 9 studies found intervals crossing zero at every site: arm 0.13 (-0.27 to 0.51), thigh 0.17 (-0.13 to 0.43), whole body -0.08 (-0.45 to 0.29). The authors read this as a small benefit from resting more than 60 seconds, and no clear further gain past 90 seconds. Six of the studies used untrained people, and they ran for only 5 to 10 weeks.. The ACSM found no strength difference between rest under and over one minute, and not enough data to say whether rest length affects growth.. An earlier review concluded that the research does not support needing shorter rest for growth than for strength.

Rest until the next set is limited by the target muscle, not by your breathing. Heavy compound lifts usually need longer to perform well. Cutting rest is a fair way to fit a session into less time. Treat it as a time choice, not as progress.
A hard session leaves a signal and leaves fatigue. How you feel in the next day or two mostly reflects the fatigue, so that is a poor time to judge your plan.

Older books draw a neat "supercompensation" curve with a perfect window for your next session. Train, recover and come back stronger is sound. A window you can time is not established. Use what you can observe instead: session performance, joint comfort, sleep, appetite and motivation. Recovery covers these.
Your body adapts to what you actually do. Heavy, low-repetition work builds the skill of lifting heavy. Plenty of hard work in a moderate range builds more size. These overlap but are not identical.
It also applies to movements. You mostly get better at the exercise you practise, so keep exercises long enough to progress on them.

People respond differently to the same training. Genes play a part. So do sleep, food, stress, history and skill, and those you can influence. Averages tell you where to start, not where you will end up. Your own log, over months, becomes the better guide.

Most of this comes from studies lasting weeks to months, mostly in young adults, often men. The direction is fairly consistent. The precision is not, which is why you will see ranges rather than exact numbers.

See a clinician. This chapter describes normal training in healthy adults. Persistent pain, unexplained loss of strength, or symptoms that do not settle with rest are not things to adjust in your training. See a qualified clinician.

Take working sets close enough that the last repetitions are hard. Failure is not required.. Muscle damage is not what drives growth. Soreness is a poor measure of progress.. Growth rises with volume, with diminishing returns. Count assisting sets as half.. With volume equal, frequency does not change growth, but it does help strength.. Rest long enough for the target muscle to limit the next set. Cutting rest is a time choice.. Early strength gains arrive first. Judge a plan over months.
Knowing which muscle does what makes every plan easier to read: why a session has the moves it has, and what to swap in when you cannot do one. Names here follow standard anatomy.

Muscle group | What it does | Main moves | Smaller moves. Muscle group: Quadriceps (front thigh); What it does: Straightens the knee; Main moves: Squat, leg press, lunge, split squat; Smaller moves: Leg extension. Muscle group: Hamstrings (back thigh); What it does: Bends the knee and extends the hip; Main moves: Romanian deadlift, deadlift; Smaller moves: Leg curl, Nordic curl. Muscle group: Calves; What it does: Point the foot; push off when walking and running; Main moves: Running, jumping; Smaller moves: Standing calf raise (gastrocnemius), seated calf raise (soleus). Muscle group: Abs (rectus abdominis); What it does: Curl the trunk; brace against bending back; Main moves: Heavy squats and deadlifts (bracing); Smaller moves: Crunch, leg raise, ab wheel. Muscle group: Obliques; What it does: Twist and bend the trunk sideways; resist twisting; Main moves: Carries, single-arm work; Smaller moves: Pallof press, side plank, cable woodchop. Muscle group: Lower back (erectors); What it does: Keep the spine straight under load; Main moves: Deadlift, squat, rows; Smaller moves: Back extension, good morning

How a full week splits the body. Push: chest, front and side shoulders, triceps · 0.33 · bench, overhead press, dips. Pull: back, rear shoulders, biceps, grip · 0.33 · rows, pull-ups, curls. Legs and trunk: quads, hamstrings, glutes, calves, abs · 0.34 · squat, hinge, lunge, core

Every balanced plan covers all three. A rough rule: about as many pulling sets as pushing sets, which keeps shoulders comfortable and posture balanced. See Building a push session, Building a pull session and Building a leg session.

Pick another move from the same row: same muscle, same job, different tool. For example, no pull-up bar: a pulldown or band-assisted pull-up. No barbell: dumbbell or machine versions. Levlofit's Workout tab lists other moves for each exercise, and Levlofit AI can make a swap stick.

Bringing up one muscle. Check the basics first · Are you eating enough and progressing on your main lifts? A muscle cannot grow without both.. Train it more often · Add 2 to 4 hard sets for it on one more day a week.. Add a direct move · If it only gets compound work, add an isolation move for it near the end of a session.. Try other rep ranges · Lighter sets of 15 to 30 reps or heavier sets of 6 to 8, taken close to failure.. Be patient · Small muscles (calves, forearms, side shoulders) change slowest; judge over 8 to 12 weeks.
Occasionally the fix is less work, not more, when recovery is the problem; that is the less common case.
Small differences between sides are normal and rarely matter. For a clear gap:

Use single-arm and single-leg moves, starting with the weaker side.. Let the weaker side set the reps and weight; the stronger side matches, no more.. Film your bilateral lifts to stop leaning or twisting toward the stronger side.
See Lagging muscles and Posture and movement.

Every muscle group has a main move and a few smaller moves; any one from the same row trains it.. Balance pushing and pulling across the week.. For a lagging muscle: eat enough, then add sets or a direct move, and give it 8 to 12 weeks.
Cardio guidelines count minutes of moderate or vigorous activity. You can judge both without a heart-rate monitor by rating your effort from 0 to 10, relative to your own fitness.

Effort | Name | What it counts toward. Effort: 2 to 4; Name: Light; What it counts toward: Everyday movement such as slow walking.. Effort: 5 to 6; Name: Moderate; What it counts toward: 150 to 300 minutes a week.. Effort: 7 to 8; Name: Vigorous; What it counts toward: 75 to 150 minutes a week.
Evidence: strong. WHO rates light activity at 2 to 4, moderate at 5 or 6 and vigorous at 7 or 8 on a 0 to 10 scale of perceived exertion, relative to each person's capacity.
One vigorous minute counts as two moderate ones.
Your week | Minutes. Your week: All moderate; Minutes: 150. Your week: All vigorous; Minutes: 75. Your week: Mixed: 90 moderate plus 30 vigorous; Minutes: 120

Moderate. Brisk walk, 30 minutes on Monday, Wednesday and Friday: 90 moderate minutes.. Vigorous. Jog, 15 minutes on Tuesday and Saturday: 30 vigorous minutes.. Add up. 90 + 2 x 30 = 150. The minimum is met.
Running uses a talk test for the same idea; see Running. Lifting uses a different scale, reps in reserve; see Exercise science.

Rate cardio effort 0 to 10: 5 or 6 is moderate, 7 or 8 is vigorous.. One vigorous minute counts like two moderate minutes toward the weekly target.. Mix both to reach at least 150 moderate-equivalent minutes a week.

passages.chapterTitle: Heart rate, sweat and calories burned
passages.text: Watches and machines give numbers for everything. Some are useful, some mislead. This chapter shows which to trust and how to use them.

passages.chapterTitle: Heart rate, sweat and calories burned
passages.text: A simple estimate of your maximum heart rate is 208 minus 0.7 times your age. It is an estimate: your real maximum can be 10 beats or more either way.

passages.chapterTitle: Heart rate, sweat and calories burned

passages.chapterTitle: Heart rate, sweat and calories burned
passages.text: 208 - 0.7 x age · bpm · estimated maximum heart rate. 187 · bpm · estimated maximum for a 30-year-old. 120 to 142 · bpm · moderate zone (64 to 76%) for that 30-year-old

passages.chapterTitle: Heart rate, sweat and calories burned
passages.text: Heart rate is most useful for steady cardio such as easy runs and cycling. During lifting and short intervals, wrist monitors lag and jump, so go by effort instead. Heat, caffeine, stress, poor sleep and illness all raise heart rate on a given day. See Easy, moderate and hard cardio.

passages.chapterTitle: Heart rate, sweat and calories burned
passages.text: What it really means. At easy effort, a higher share of the energy you use comes from fat.. Harder effort burns more energy per minute, so often as much fat or more in the same time.. Easy effort lets you go longer and recover faster.. What people think it means. Easy cardio burns more fat in total.. You must stay in the zone to lose fat.. Hard cardio is wasted for fat loss.

passages.chapterTitle: Heart rate, sweat and calories burned
passages.text: Fat loss depends on your energy balance over days and weeks, not on the zone of one session. Choose the cardio you can do regularly. See Calories and body composition.

passages.chapterTitle: Heart rate, sweat and calories burned
passages.text: Sweat cools you down. How much you sweat depends on heat, humidity, your genes, body size and fitness; fitter people often start sweating sooner. A dry session can be a great one, and a dripping one can be easy. To manage heavy sweating: train in cooler hours, wear light clothes, carry a towel, and replace fluid and salt on long or hot days. See Hydration and electrolytes.

passages.chapterTitle: Heart rate, sweat and calories burned

passages.chapterTitle: Heart rate, sweat and calories burned
passages.text: In a test of seven popular wrist devices, heart rate was fairly accurate but none measured energy burned well; even the best was off by about a quarter. Gym machines and class estimates use averages that ignore your size and fitness, so they are no better. Treat calories-burned numbers as rough, and never "eat back" all of them. Judge your intake by the trend in your body weight instead.

passages.chapterTitle: Heart rate, sweat and calories burned
passages.text: Mixing the two well. Cardio does not kill gains · Adding cardio to lifting does not reduce muscle growth overall; very large amounts of running may slightly reduce leg strength gains.. Do the priority first · Whatever you most want to improve goes first in the session, while you are fresh.. Separate hard sessions · Hard intervals and heavy leg days are best on different days, or 6 hours or more apart.. Eat for both · Cardio uses energy; if you are trying to gain, eat a little more to cover it.

passages.chapterTitle: Heart rate, sweat and calories burned
passages.text: For general health it does not matter much which comes first; for strength goals, lift first. See Combining different kinds of training.

Sweat cools you; it does not measure effort.. Calories-burned numbers are rough; trust your weight trend.. Lift first when strength is the goal; cardio helps, it does not kill gains.
Good technique means repeating the same movement, under control, through a range you own. Learn each lift light, and add weight only when every rep looks and feels the same.

Pattern | Example | Main muscles. Pattern: Squat; Example: Goblet squat; Main muscles: Thighs and hips. Pattern: Hinge; Example: Romanian deadlift; Main muscles: Hamstrings, hips and back. Pattern: Push; Example: Push-up, bench press; Main muscles: Chest, shoulders and triceps. Pattern: Pull; Example: Row, pull-up; Main muscles: Back and biceps. Pattern: Single leg; Example: Split squat, step-up; Main muscles: Legs and balance. Pattern: Carry; Example: Farmers carry; Main muscles: Grip and trunk
Levlofit rules. These are Levlofit coaching rules, not research findings; technique coaching is hard to test in trials. A qualified coach can check your form in person.

Start light. Bodyweight, a light dumbbell or an empty bar.. Same setup. Place your feet, hands and grip the same way on every rep.. Control the way down. Lower the weight under control instead of dropping into the bottom.. Use the range you own. Go as deep as you can while keeping your position, without pain.. Check it. Film one set from the side and compare it with the exercise demo.. Then add weight. Only when every rep looks the same, keeping 2 to 3 reps in reserve while you learn.

Ready for more weight | Fix before adding weight. Ready for more weight: Every rep has the same speed and shape; Fix before adding weight: Reps change shape or speed as the set goes on. Ready for more weight: You finish the set with reps in reserve; Fix before adding weight: You reach failure earlier than planned. Ready for more weight: No pain in any joint, during or the next day; Fix before adding weight: Joint pain during or after the lift; see Injury prevention
The practice loop is simple: learn it light, repeat it often, film and check, then add a little.

Six patterns cover most training: squat, hinge, push, pull, single leg and carry.. Learn each lift light with the same setup and a controlled way down.. Add weight only when every rep looks the same and nothing hurts.

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: The first weeks decide whether you keep going. Most worries beginners have are common, normal and easy to handle once you know what to expect.

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: What it feels like. Everyone is watching me.. They are judging how little I lift.. I do not belong here.. What is usually true. Most people are focused on their own sets and their phone.. Every strong person started light; many remember being new.. A gym is for anyone who trains, at any level.

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: Making the first visits easier. Go at quiet hours · Mid-morning or early afternoon is calmer than 6 to 8 pm.. Arrive with a plan · Open today's session in Levlofit so you always know the next move.. Start with what you know · Machines and dumbbells first; add barbell lifts as you learn them.. Keep going back · Comfort comes from repetition: by the fourth or fifth visit it feels normal.

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: Re-rack your weights and wipe down benches and handles after use.. Do not stand directly in front of someone's mirror view or rest on a machine between long phone breaks.. Ask "how many sets left?" before working in on equipment.. Do not give advice to people who did not ask, even about form. You do not know their goals, injuries or programme, and it usually comes across as rude. If someone is putting others in danger, tell the staff.

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: You do not need a trainer for every lift. Many people learn well from good videos and practice.

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: Learning a lift on your own. Watch · Watch a clear demonstration (Levlofit's exercise library shows each move) from front and side.. Practise light · Start with an empty bar, light dumbbells or a bodyweight version.. Film yourself · Record from the side. What you feel and what you do are often different.. Compare · Check your video against the demonstration and fix one thing at a time.. Get help when stuck · A coach for one session is worth it if a lift hurts or stays wrong after a few weeks.

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: See Learning a lift.

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: Strength and muscle come back faster than they took to build the first time, but your joints and tendons need a week or two to catch up.

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: Weight to start with after a break. 0 · 50 · Break of 6 months or more: start here and add weight each session [% of your old working weight]. 50 · 70 · Break of 1 to 6 months [% of your old working weight]. 70 · 90 · Break of 2 to 4 weeks [% of your old working weight]. 90 · 100 · Break under 2 weeks: pick up where you left off [% of your old working weight]

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: These are Levlofit's starting rules, not research limits. Expect to be back near your old numbers within weeks. Beginner-style fast progress is not something you can "waste"; if you are weak now, you will improve fast now.

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: One weak session means little: poor sleep, a heavy or empty stomach, stress, dehydration or simply a bad day. Everyone has them, from beginners to elite lifters. Log it, go home, and come back for the next planned session. Look for a cause only when sessions are poor for two weeks or more. See Breaking through plateaus.

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: Should I train today?. Fever, body aches, chest congestion or stomach illness? · Rest. Train again 1 to 2 days after the fever is gone. · Go on to the next question.. Only a runny nose or mild sore throat? · Light training is usually fine; drop the weight and stop if you feel worse. · Train as planned.

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: This is common practical advice, not a research rule. If you are contagious, stay home for the sake of everyone else, and wipe down what you touch. Any chest pain, fainting or unusual breathlessness means stop and see a doctor.

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: Probably normal soreness. Starts 24 to 48 hours after training. A dull, spread-out ache in the muscle. Eases over 2 to 4 days. Moving gently helps. Possibly an injury. Starts during the session, often suddenly. Sharp, in one spot, or in a joint. Lasts more than about 4 days, or gets worse. Swelling, bruising, clicking with pain, or weakness

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: Train through mild soreness with a good warm-up; it usually eases as you move. Not being sore does not mean the session failed: soreness only means something was new. See Muscle soreness and Injury prevention. See a doctor or physiotherapist for anything in the right-hand column.

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: On deadlifts and rows, your grip often fails before your back or legs. Your grip should not decide how heavy you train those lifts.

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: Fixes, in order. Chalk · Dry hands hold far better; liquid chalk is allowed in more gyms.. Grip the bar low · Hold it in the fingers near the palm crease, not in the middle of the palm, to stop skin pinching.. Hook or mixed grip · Thumb under the fingers, or one palm forward and one back, for heavy sets.. Straps · For your heaviest sets; strong lifters use them without shame.. Train grip directly · Dead hangs, farmer's carries and heavy holds, once or twice a week.

passages.chapterTitle: Your first weeks at the gym
passages.text: Nerves fade with repetition; go at quiet hours with a plan.. Learn lifts with videos, light weights and filming yourself.. After a break, start lighter and build back for a week or two.. One bad session means nothing; rest when you have a fever or chest symptoms.. Sharp pain during a session is not soreness: stop and get it checked.

A warm-up has one well-supported benefit: a better session. Other benefits are claimed on much weaker grounds. This chapter separates them and gives you a warm-up short enough that you will keep doing it.
Mobility is here because the two get confused. A warm-up prepares you for today. Mobility work changes your range over months.
The aim is to get ready, not tired.

What it does | How. What it does: Raises muscle temperature; How: Light continuous activity.. What it does: Rehearses the movement; How: Practising the exact lift with gradually heavier loads.. What it does: Tests the day; How: Rising loads show how today is going before a hard set.

Evidence: emerging. A review of passive heating, such as baths, saunas and heated clothing, found warmer muscle develops force faster. Maximal voluntary force did not rise. A warmer muscle gets to a force sooner. It does not become stronger. This review did not study active warm-ups, which do much more than raise temperature.

Claimed benefit | Grade | What is supported. Claimed benefit: Better performance today; Grade: Moderate; What is supported: Dynamic stretching improves jumping and sprinting compared with no warm-up. This is the benefit to rely on.. Claimed benefit: Faster force; Grade: Emerging; What is supported: Warmer muscle produces force faster, without raising maximal force.. Claimed benefit: More range today; Grade: Moderate; What is supported: A single session of static stretching reduces stiffness.. Claimed benefit: Feeling ready; Grade: Practical; What is supported: A real benefit that research has not settled. Use it if it helps.. Claimed benefit: Less injury; Grade: Not settled; What is supported: Do not treat this as your reason to warm up. See below.

Injury risk. "Warm up so you do not get injured" is the most repeated reason, and not a secure one. Do not count on a warm-up or stretching to protect you.. The stronger evidence points to strength training itself. Across six randomised trials with 7,738 people aged 12 to 40, it cut sports injury risk by about two thirds (relative risk 0.338, 0.238 to 0.480), and more training was linked with more protection. Most of those people were athletes, so applying this to gym training is a reasonable step, not a tested one.
Dynamic stretching moves a joint through its range under control, such as leg swings, arm circles, bodyweight squats and walking lunges. Static stretching holds a stretched position still.

Approach | Effect on jumping and sprinting. Approach: Dynamic alone; Effect on jumping and sprinting: Improved jump height and sprint time. The steady choice.. Approach: Static, then dynamic; Effect on jumping and sprinting: Ranked highest for jump height, and clearly better than no warm-up.. Approach: Static alone, just before; Effect on jumping and sprinting: Ranked lowest for jump height, and made sprint time worse.. Approach: Foam rolling; Effect on jumping and sprinting: No significant difference from no warm-up.

Evidence: moderate. This comes from a network analysis of 35 studies, with dynamic stretching for 7 to 10 minutes showing the largest effect. Most studies were not randomised and few used blinding, so treat the ranking as a guide.. Hold length matters too. Static stretching of 60 seconds or more per muscle cut performance by 4.6%, against 1.1% for under 60 seconds.
In practice:

If a stretch lets you reach a position you otherwise cannot, use it, keep it short, then do dynamic movement and warm-up sets.. If you have no such limit, dynamic work alone is enough and faster.. Avoid long static holds as your only preparation right before heavy or explosive work.
These studies measured jumping and sprinting, which may react more than an ordinary set of 8 to 12 repetitions.

Stage | Time | Purpose. Stage: General; Time: 3 to 5 min; Purpose: Light continuous activity to raise temperature.. Stage: Dynamic mobility; Time: 4 to 6 min; Purpose: Controlled movement through the ranges you will use today.. Stage: Activation; Time: 0 to 5 min; Purpose: Optional light work for muscles you struggle to feel.. Stage: Warm-up sets; Time: 5 to 10 min; Purpose: Your first big lift, with gradually heavier loads.

These times are practical guides. Warm-up sets matter most, and they are the stage people skip. They rehearse the exact movement, and they tell you something: when a normal load feels heavy today, you find out before committing to a hard set. If you are short of time, cut the general stage, not these.

On activation drills. Glute bridges before squats and band work before pressing are popular and cheap. It is not established that they add anything beyond warm-up sets. Keep them if they help you. Drop them before you drop your warm-up sets.
Later exercises in a session need only one or two light sets.
Mobility is the range you can actively reach and control. Range you can only be pushed into is not much use under load.

Evidence: moderate. A review of 65 studies found stretching does not lengthen muscle: fascicle length did not change after one session or many. Stiffness fell after both. Tolerance to the stretch rose only after repeated stretching.. Regular stretching builds range, and in one review its volume, intensity and frequency did not play a significant role in how much.. Strength training through a full range gave range of motion gains similar to stretching.
What this means for you:

Train mobility separately. A warm-up uses the range you have. New range takes weeks to months.. Pick a method you will keep up. Regular practice matters. Exact hold times matter less than people claim.. Lift through your full range. It builds usable range while you train anyway.. Target the real limit. A muscle can feel tight without being what limits you. Test one position, work on it, and retest weeks later.
Stretching into pain. Mild discomfort is expected. Sharp, radiating or joint-line pain is not. Stop, and see a qualified clinician rather than stretching harder.

Session | Focus | Typical movements. Session: Push; Focus: Shoulders, chest, triceps, upper back; Typical movements: Arm circles, band pull-aparts, upper back rotations, push-up variations. Session: Pull; Focus: Lats, upper back, rear shoulders; Typical movements: Shoulder blade drills, dead hangs, light rows. Session: Legs; Focus: Hips, knees, ankles, glutes; Typical movements: Bodyweight squats, walking lunges, leg swings, ankle rocks

Skipping warm-up sets to save time. Your first hard set becomes the warm-up.. Long static holds as your only preparation. Follow them with dynamic work.. Warming up until tired. Getting breathless uses energy your working sets need.. Treating foam rolling as a performance boost. Use it if it makes a position more comfortable.. Expecting a warm-up to fix a mobility limit. That takes months.. Relying on the warm-up for injury protection. The evidence points to strength training.

The demonstrated benefit of warming up is a better session.. Warmer muscle produces force faster, not more maximal force.. Dynamic work helps. Long static holds alone just before explosive work do not.. Warm-up sets matter most and double as a recovery check. Activation drills are optional.. Stretching does not lengthen muscle. Range improves through lower stiffness and more tolerance.. Protection from injury is better supported for strength training than for warming up.
A muscle adapts to the demand it faces. Once it has, that same demand only maintains it. Progressive overload means raising the demand often enough that adapting stays necessary.
This chapter is about the bookkeeping: raising the demand over months without collecting more fatigue or risk than the gains are worth. Most of it is practical guidance, labelled as such.

"Add weight to the bar" is one method. For a beginner it is usually the best one, but it is not the real requirement. The requirement is that the hard, well-performed work a muscle does should trend up over time.
An extra repetition, an extra hard set, or the same work through a fuller range all count. You will need them eventually, because load cannot climb forever.
In practice. If you cannot say what improved since last week, perhaps nothing did. Log your sets. Without a log, training drifts into repeating work you have already adapted to.

Variable | What it does | When to use it. Variable: Load; What it does: Raises the demand of each repetition directly.; When to use it: First choice for beginners and big lifts with small weight steps.. Variable: Repetitions; What it does: More work at the same load. Bridges big jumps in weight.; When to use it: When the next weight step is too big to take cleanly.. Variable: Hard sets; What it does: Raises weekly volume, which has a clear link to growth, but costs the most recovery and time.; When to use it: Over months, when load and repetitions slow and you have recovery to spare.. Variable: Range of motion; What it does: More work per repetition.; When to use it: Early, then always. Treat full range as the standard.. Variable: Effort; What it does: Recovers what a too-easy set left behind. Failure has not been shown to add more.; When to use it: When sets are stopped well short of hard. It runs out quickly.. Variable: Technique; What it does: Puts the load on the muscle you mean to train.; When to use it: Always. Everything else depends on it.
These are not a menu to rotate for variety. Over the long term: technique and range first, then load and repetitions together, then volume, then effort as a controlled adjustment.

Cutting rest. Shorter rest makes a session feel much harder, which is why it gets mistaken for progress. With less rest you usually do less work on the next set, and recording that as improvement is a bookkeeping error.. It is also not proven to cost you muscle. A review of 9 studies found intervals crossing zero, with a small benefit past 60 seconds and no clear gain past 90. The ACSM found not enough data on rest and growth. So cutting rest is not progress, and short rest does not ruin your results.. Log it as fitting the session into less time.
Three more things look like progress and are not:

Adding exercises. A longer session is not a harder one for each muscle. Exercises that repeat a pattern add fatigue and time.. Changing the plan. Something new brings soreness and a fresh feeling, and it resets your numbers, so real progress becomes impossible to see.. Adding load by shortening range. A heavier partial repetition is a different, easier exercise with the same name.
Double progression is the default here because it prevents a very common mistake: adding load before you own the current one.

Give each exercise a repetition range, not a fixed number.. Keep the load the same and add repetitions until every working set reaches the top of the range with good technique.. Only then add load. Your repetitions fall back toward the bottom of the range, and the cycle repeats.
Technique sets the top of the range. A repetition with a changed movement path does not count.
Here is an example: a range of 8 to 10, three sets, on incline dumbbell press with dumbbells rising in 2.5 kg steps.

Week | Load | Repetitions per set | Decision. Week: 1; Load: 20 kg; Repetitions per set: 8, 8, 8; Decision: Keep the load. Add repetitions.. Week: 2; Load: 20 kg; Repetitions per set: 9, 8, 8; Decision: Keep the load.. Week: 3; Load: 20 kg; Repetitions per set: 10, 9, 8; Decision: Keep the load. Not every set is at the top.. Week: 4; Load: 20 kg; Repetitions per set: 10, 10, 10; Decision: Range complete. Add load next session.. Week: 5; Load: 22.5 kg; Repetitions per set: 8, 8, 7; Decision: Expected. Start the cycle again.

Week 5 is where people give up. Repetitions falling after a load increase is the method working. Other approaches work too, but this one needs no percentages, no maximum tests, and no maths beyond reading your own log.

Take the smallest load increase available. A 5 kg jump on a heavy squat is a small percentage. The same 5 kg on a lateral raise is huge, which is why small-muscle exercises often stall. When the jump is too big:

Add repetitions until you are comfortably past the top of your range, then jump.. Add the new load to one set at a time over several sessions.. Use small fractional plates on barbell lifts if your gym has them.

Slowing down is normal. Beginners may add load almost every session. Later, progress can take months. Reading a normal slowdown as a broken plan often leads you to break it. Check the cheap explanations first:

Check | What a problem looks like. Check: Sleep; What a problem looks like: Short or broken sleep in the weeks before the stall.. Check: Food; What a problem looks like: Body weight flat or falling while you are trying to gain muscle.. Check: Consistency; What a problem looks like: Sessions missed or cut short. Count what you completed, not what you planned.. Check: Effort; What a problem looks like: Sets ending several repetitions short of hard while logged as hard.. Check: Fatigue; What a problem looks like: Several exercises falling at once, with poor sleep, low motivation or joint aches.
A stall on one exercise is an exercise problem. A stall on most exercises at once points to recovery, and more work is the wrong answer. Plateaus covers true stalls.

Adding load by calendar instead of performance. Technique slips to absorb it, and your log records progress your muscle never saw.. Treating every session as a test. Most sessions should be repeatable, not maximal.. Changing exercises before progressing on them. Progress needs a stable reference.. Expecting every exercise to climb together. Big lifts and small ones do not move at the same pace.. Logging what you meant to do. Record what happened, including bad sets. A log of only good days cannot show a stall.

Hard, well-performed work must trend up. Load is one way, not the definition.. Cutting rest, adding exercises, changing plans and shortening range are not progress.. Double progression: fill the repetition range, then add load.. Use the smallest step available. The percentage jump is what matters.. Check sleep, food, consistency and effort before deciding a plan has failed.

A programme is a set of sessions with rules for when to add weight, reps or sets. Following a proven one beats making it up as you go: it balances the body, spaces out recovery, and tells you exactly what to do next. Many good programmes work; the one you keep doing is the best one. Levlofit builds yours from your goals, days, equipment and level.

A proven programme. Structure that fits your week. Rest between hard sessions for the same muscles. A rule for progress, so you keep getting stronger. Every major muscle covered. Effort set for your level. Making it up each day. Sessions that depend on your mood. Some muscles hit three days running, others never. The same weights for months. Lots of chest and arms, little back and legs. Sessions that are too easy or too punishing

Picking a starting point. New to strength training, or back after a long break? · Start with a simple full-body plan, 2 or 3 days a week, for about 3 months. · Go on to the next question.. Can you train 4 or more days a week? · An upper/lower or push/pull/legs split, each muscle twice a week. · Full body, 2 or 3 days a week.
The two things that matter most are the days you can really train and the equipment you can really use. After that, effort and consistency decide results far more than the programme's name.

Full body. Each session trains the whole body. Best with 2 or 3 days a week. Each muscle 2 to 3 times a week. Ideal for beginners, who recover fast. Split (upper/lower, push/pull/legs). Each session trains part of the body. Best with 4 to 6 days a week. Each muscle about twice a week when well designed. Suits more sets per muscle as you advance

For muscle growth, training a muscle at least twice a week works better than once, when total sets are equal. For strength, frequency matters little once weekly sets are the same, so pick the layout that fits your week. A split that hits each muscle only once a week ("bro split") wastes a beginner's fast recovery.
These are widely used and known to work. Levlofit does not copy them; it uses the same principles.

Type | What it looks like | Who it suits. Type: Simple linear progression; What it looks like: 3 full-body days a week, alternating two sessions of 5 main lifts; add a little weight every session while you can; Who it suits: Complete beginners, first 3 months. Type: Tiered linear progression (the GZCLP style); What it looks like: Each day: one heavy main lift, one lighter secondary lift, then accessories; when you miss reps, change sets and reps before cutting weight; Who it suits: Beginners after the first months. Type: Wave on a training max (the 5/3/1 style); What it looks like: Work from 90% of an estimated max; three-week waves of 5, 3 and 1 rep sets, then extra lighter sets and accessories; raise the max a little each cycle; Who it suits: Late beginners and up, who want steady long-term progress. Type: Push/pull/legs; What it looks like: 6 days: push, pull, legs, twice each, with main lifts and accessories; Who it suits: Those with time and good recovery. Type: Dumbbell-only plan; What it looks like: Full body or push/pull/legs with dumbbells and bodyweight; Who it suits: Home trainees without a barbell. Type: Bodyweight plan; What it looks like: Push-up, pull-up, dip, squat and core progressions that get harder by lever, not weight; Who it suits: No equipment

Ways a programme moves you forward. More weight · The classic: add the smallest step when every set reaches the top of the rep range.. More reps · Same weight, one or two more reps. Counts as real progress.. More sets · An extra set for a muscle that is lagging, when recovery allows.. Better technique · Deeper, slower, steadier reps with the same weight.
Expect stalls. When one lift stalls for two or three sessions, take 10% off and build back up with more reps. See Progressive overload and Breaking through plateaus.

What different rep ranges are best at. 1 to 5 · Maximal strength · Heaviest loads; most skill practice for heavy lifts; long rests.. 6 to 12 · Muscle and strength together · The most time-efficient range for most people.. 12 to 20 · Muscle, endurance · Builds as much muscle as heavier sets when taken close to failure; burns more.. 20 to 30 or more · Muscle, endurance · Works too, but sets are long and uncomfortable.

Light and heavy sets build similar muscle when each set ends close to failure; heavy sets build more maximal strength. No rep range "tones" or "burns fat": fat loss comes from eating less. Most good programmes mix ranges.

How close to failure to stop. 0 · 1 · Failure: fine on safe isolation moves now and then [reps left in reserve]. 1 · 3 · Where most sets should end: close enough to grow [reps left in reserve]. 3 · 5 · Good for heavy compound lifts while learning technique [reps left in reserve]. 5 · 8 · Too easy to drive much growth [reps left in reserve]

Sets stopped 1 to 3 reps short of failure build about as much muscle as sets to failure, with less fatigue. People misjudge how close they are, so take a set to failure now and then on a safe move to calibrate. Beginners should not grind squats, deadlifts or presses to failure while learning them.
Ask these questions about any plan, from a website, a friend or a trainer:

Does it train every major muscle group about twice a week?. Does it have a clear rule for adding weight, reps or sets?. Are the weekly sets reasonable: roughly 10 to 20 hard sets per muscle for most people?. Does it fit the days and time you really have?. Does it include some cardio and rest days?
If most answers are yes, follow it for at least 3 months before judging it. If it is a long list of random exercises with no progression rule, choose another.

Stay on one programme for at least 3 to 6 months. Change when you have stalled for weeks despite good sleep and food, when your goal changes, or when your schedule does. Changing every few weeks resets your progress tracking and is the most common reason people spin their wheels.

Follow a proven plan; the best one is the one you will keep doing.. Beginners do best on full body, 2 or 3 days a week; each muscle at least twice a week.. Any rep range builds muscle when sets end 1 to 3 reps short of failure.. Progress by weight, reps, sets or better technique, and stay with a plan for months.
Rest is one input to recovery. Recovery is the outcome: fatigue clears, and the signal from training turns into adaptation.
This chapter covers what has real evidence, says where the evidence is thinner than the fitness industry suggests, and gives you signals you can actually watch.

A hard session creates a signal to adapt, and it creates fatigue. What you feel in the next day or two is mostly the fatigue. Recovery depends on sleep, on eating enough, and on not stacking another big demand too soon.
Without a real training signal, sleep and protein have nothing to act on. Recovery decides how much of the signal is carried out.
Sleep has clear evidence behind it for training performance, and it is often the first thing people trade away.

Evidence: moderate. A review of 69 publications found sleep loss lowered exercise performance by about 7.6% on average, across every category tested. Performance fell about 0.4% for each extra hour awake before exercise. The effects were consistent for going without sleep or waking earlier than normal, and less consistent for going to bed late. Results varied widely between studies and 89% of participants were men, so the size for any one person is uncertain.

One finding helps with planning: afternoon and evening sessions after a poor night consistently suffered, while morning sessions were largely unaffected. If a bad night is unavoidable, train earlier if you can.

Evidence: insufficient on sleep and injury. You will often hear that poor sleep raises injury risk. A review of 12 cohort studies concluded that current evidence does not support poor sleep as an independent risk factor for injury in adult athletes, while noting the studies were too mixed to settle the question.
This is no argument for sleeping less. The case for sleep rests on performance, which has good support.
These are practical habits, not findings from the papers above.

Keep your wake time steady, including at weekends.. Give yourself enough time in bed. You control that directly.. Keep your room dark and cool.. If late caffeine or alcohol affects your sleep, move or drop it.

Recovery has a material cost. Energy decides whether your body has resources to build. Gaining muscle while eating well below your needs is possible in some situations and harder in others. Protein supplies what repair and building use. Protein gives the amounts and Indian sources.
The biggest recovery lever you control is how much you asked for in training.

Lever | Effect on recovery demand. Lever: Weekly hard sets; Effect on recovery demand: The main driver. More volume brings more signal and more cost.. Lever: Closeness to failure; Effect on recovery demand: Failure adds fatigue, and has not been shown to give consistently better results.. Lever: Exercise choice; Effect on recovery demand: In practice, heavy compound lifts tire you more per set than machine isolation work.. Lever: Spreading sets out; Effect on recovery demand: The same weekly sets over more days can keep later sets from fading.

Rest days are part of the plan. They need not be still: walking and ordinary activity are fine. They do need to be easier than a training day. A "light" day that becomes a hard session is an unlogged training day.

Exams, work and personal pressure can reduce how much training you can handle, even if your plan has not changed. In practice, let volume move with your life. Cutting sets during a hard month and restoring them later keeps you consistent. Holding volume and missing sessions does not.

No home device directly measures recovery. Treat sleep scores and readiness numbers as weak inputs, and do not let them overrule your logged performance. These practical signals are cheaper and more useful:

Signal | Recovering well | Under-recovered. Signal: Session performance; Recovering well: Load or repetitions rising over weeks, with an occasional flat day; Under-recovered: Several unrelated exercises falling for over a week. Signal: Warm-up; Recovering well: Warm-up sets feel normal; Under-recovered: Normal warm-up loads feel heavy. Signal: Joints; Recovering well: Quiet, or briefly stiff then fine; Under-recovered: Aches that outlast sessions and build week to week. Signal: Sleep; Recovering well: Falling asleep normally, waking fairly rested; Under-recovered: Trouble falling asleep, or waking early despite being tired. Signal: Appetite and mood; Recovering well: Steady; Under-recovered: Both low for several days with no other reason
One bad session is noise. A week of them across several exercises, plus two or more other rows, is worth acting on. See Deload week.

Soreness is not a recovery reading. It often reflects unfamiliar work.. Recovery tools are not recovery. Do not expect massage guns or similar tools to replace sleep and food. Regular cold-water immersion had a harmful effect on strength gains from resistance training in one review (effect size -0.60, -0.87 to -0.33), so avoid making it a habit if strength is your goal.. Total inactivity is not required. Light movement is fine.. Supplements do not replace the basics. They do not make up for too little sleep or food.

Beyond a training adjustment. Ordinary fatigue responds to less training. These do not. See a qualified clinician:. Sharp, localised or lasting pain, especially at rest or at night.. Numbness, tingling or weakness in a specific pattern.. Fatigue, unexplained weight loss or falling performance that continues after several weeks of truly reduced training.. Missed periods, frequent illness or bone pain alongside low food intake. These may point to low energy availability, which is a medical concern.. Distress about food, weight or missed sessions that affects daily life.. This Handbook does not diagnose and does not replace individual care.

Recovery turns a training signal into adaptation.. Sleep loss lowers performance, more so for afternoon and evening sessions.. It is not established that poor sleep alone raises injury risk.. Your biggest recovery lever is how much you asked for in training.. Soreness and readiness scores are weak signals. Logged performance across exercises is stronger.. Lasting pain, nerve symptoms or fatigue that survives real rest are medical questions.

A push session trains the muscles that press weight away from you: chest, front and side shoulders, and triceps. They work together, which makes the grouping convenient. Nothing requires you to train them this way.
Your Levlofit plan builds your sessions for you. This chapter teaches the reasoning, so you can judge a session, swap an exercise sensibly, or build one for your own equipment.
Think of a session as an ordered set of slots, each with a job. Two arguments support this, resting on different evidence.

Order. The ACSM found strength was better when an exercise was trained at the beginning of a session rather than the end. Exercise order did not affect muscle growth. So put what you most want to get stronger at first.
Coverage. Different exercises can grow different parts of a muscle.

Evidence: emerging. In 30 trained people who trained each leg differently for 8 weeks, leg extensions favoured one part of the quadriceps and leg press favoured another. This is one lower-body study. Applying it to pressing muscles is reasoning, not a tested result.

Slot | Job. Slot: Main press; Job: The heaviest, most technical press, done first.. Slot: Second press; Job: Another pressing angle, or a more supported press, adding work at lower technical cost.. Slot: Chest isolation; Job: A single-joint movement for the chest.. Slot: Side shoulder; Job: Lateral raises, because pressing gives side shoulders little direct work.. Slot: Triceps; Job: Direct work, after presses have already tired them.
This is a checklist for coverage, not a law.
A slot names a job, not an exercise. Apply these in order:

Equipment. Start with what you actually have.. Joints and injury history. Remove anything that irritates a known problem.. Skill. If you have less experience, prefer a shorter learning curve for the same job.. Fatigue. Free weights ask more of your stabilising muscles. That is easiest to afford early. Later, a machine often lets you keep working the target muscle for less overall fatigue.

Evidence: insufficient on free weights and machines for growth. The ACSM found strength was not affected by free weights versus machines, and not enough data to say about growth. It also concludes that many forms of resistance training work.
So choose the version you can load progressively and do consistently.
Two exercises can replace each other when both are the same movement pattern and load the same joint action.

A flat barbell bench press and an incline dumbbell press are both presses using the shoulder and elbow in the same way. A cable fly is not a substitute for either. It targets the same muscle, but the elbow stays largely fixed, so it belongs in the isolation slot.
Use this test on any exercise, including ones this Handbook does not name.

Volume is hard sets per muscle per week, with assisting sets counted as half. Every press also counts as triceps work. The ACSM found growth was enhanced by 10 or more sets per muscle group per week, and a separate review found diminishing returns as sets rise. Reach about 10 if you can, then adjust based on recovery.

Effort is how close you get to failure. Make the final repetitions truly hard. Failure is not required, and it has not been shown to give consistently better results. Exercise science sets out the evidence.
Frequency is how often you train a muscle. For strength, the ACSM found 2 or more sessions a week helped, and could not determine an upper limit. With volume equal, frequency did not change growth.
There is no established fixed recovery time such as 48 hours. It varies with the person, the exercise and the work done. Use the signals in Recovery.
These dials add up. Raising volume without thinking about effort and frequency is a common route to a plan you cannot recover from.
Nothing supports shorter rest as better. A small benefit appears past about 60 seconds, with no clear further gain past 90. The ACSM found no strength difference, and not enough data on growth.
Rest until the target muscle, not your breathing, limits the next set. Heavy presses usually need longer than isolation work to perform well.

Model | How it works | Best for. Model: Double progression; How it works: Fill a repetition range at one load, then add load.; Best for: Most muscle-building work. Repetitions absorb good and bad days.. Model: Load progression; How it works: Add load at a fixed, usually low, repetition target.; Best for: Strength work. The ACSM links loads of 80% of your one-repetition maximum or more with greater strength gains.. Model: Adjusting by feel; How it works: Change load or sets based on how today's sets went.; Best for: Weeks where your recovery varies a lot.
Match the model to your goal and repetition range. Load affects strength, but growth was not affected by loads from 30% to 100% of your maximum in the ACSM review. Heavier is not required for size.

Warm-up and mobility covers the evidence. For a push session: a few minutes of light activity, shoulder and upper back movement, then gradually heavier warm-up sets of your main press. Warm-up sets matter most. If time is short, cut the general part.
Plan recovery by which muscles you trained and how hard, not by session names. A chest day and a shoulder day share shoulder and triceps work whatever they are called.
This is one complete example, not a prescription. It fills the slots above so you can check your own reasoning.

Slot | Exercise | Sets | Repetitions | Rest. Slot: Main press; Exercise: Incline dumbbell press; Sets: 4; Repetitions: 6 to 8; Rest: 2 to 3 min. Slot: Second press; Exercise: Machine chest press; Sets: 3; Repetitions: 8 to 10; Rest: 2 min. Slot: Chest isolation; Exercise: Cable high-to-low fly; Sets: 3; Repetitions: 10 to 12; Rest: 90 sec. Slot: Side shoulder; Exercise: Dumbbell lateral raise; Sets: 3; Repetitions: 12 to 15; Rest: 60 to 90 sec. Slot: Side shoulder; Exercise: Cable lateral raise; Sets: 3; Repetitions: 12 to 15; Rest: 60 to 90 sec. Slot: Triceps; Exercise: Overhead cable triceps extension; Sets: 3; Repetitions: 10 to 12; Rest: 75 to 90 sec. Slot: Triceps; Exercise: Rope pushdown; Sets: 3; Repetitions: 12 to 15; Rest: 60 to 90 sec

Count it per muscle: chest gets 10 direct sets, side shoulders get 6, and triceps get 6 direct sets plus half of the 7 press sets, about 9.5. Chest reaches 10 in this one session. Rest figures are ranges because the evidence does not support exact numbers.

A leg session trains your quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes and calves. These include some of your largest muscles, and their big lifts are among the hardest most people do, so order matters a lot.

Go from the heaviest, most technical lift down to single-joint work that handles fatigue well. Include a squat pattern and a hip hinge, because they load the front and back of your leg in different ways.

Evidence: emerging. Thirty trained people did different exercises with each leg, twice a week for 8 weeks. Leg extension favoured the rectus femoris, part of the quadriceps. Leg press favoured the vastus lateralis, another part. Straight-leg calf raises favoured one calf muscle, the medial gastrocnemius, with no clear result for the lateral gastrocnemius or soleus. So big lifts may not make isolation work unnecessary, and the reverse may be true too.

A barbell back squat and a hack squat can replace each other. Both are squat patterns using your knees and hips. A leg press cannot replace a Romanian deadlift: one is a squat pattern and the other a hinge. Swapping them leaves the hinge slot empty.
Full range is the default. The ACSM found strength improved with a complete range of motion, though it found not enough data on range and growth. Load gained by shortening your range is not progress.
"Partial repetitions are always wrong" goes too far, though.

Evidence: moderate for long over short; insufficient for partials over full range. The advantage was clear at the far and central parts of the muscle.. The review compared these two partial ranges with each other. It does not show that partials beat a full range.
In practice:

Train through a full range by default.. A partial done on purpose in the stretched position is a fair tool, such as when a joint limits the other part of the range.. The three models from the push chapter apply. Adjusting by feel can suit squats and hinges, since it may catch a tired day before your technique breaks down.

For strength, the ACSM links loads of 80% of your one-repetition maximum or more with greater gains. For growth, load from 30% to 100% made no difference, which is how a leg extension can build quadriceps despite a modest number on the stack.

Variation is a tool for specific problems, not something your plan needs on a schedule. This chapter covers when changing an exercise is worth it, what it costs, and what a second good selection looks like.

Evidence: moderate. The ACSM found periodised programmes were not significantly better than non-periodised ones for healthy adults, given good progressive overload, and concluded periodisation is less important than once thought. It found not enough data to say whether varied exercise selection affects growth, and concluded that many forms of resistance training work.
So if variation is not needed, changing an exercise should have a real reason. "It has been a while" is not one.

Two other popular reasons are also weak. It is not established that repeating a movement harms your joints when technique and recovery are sound, or that variation protects them. Feeling fresher is a real reason, as a preference. A plan you will follow beats a slightly better one you abandon.

Progress needs a stable reference. An exercise changed every few weeks cannot show improvement, because there is no unbroken run of numbers. A new movement also takes practice, so at first your coordination may limit you before your muscle does.
If you are still progressing on an exercise, keep it.

Split squats, lunges, single-leg presses and single-leg hinges are often sold as better than two-leg work. The evidence is more specific.

Training one side at a time does show what each side can do. That follows from how it is done. It is not established that this corrects a difference between your sides better than two-leg work does.
Small side-to-side differences are common. Marked, lasting or painful ones are a reason to see a clinician, not to add more single-leg sets.
Good reasons to use single-leg work are practical: limited equipment, a spine-loading limit, preference, and seeing each side in your log.
