A deload is a planned or chosen period of less training stress. The idea is near-universal among coaches: build up fatigue, pull back, return fresher. It is also under-researched, and this chapter keeps what is reasoned, what coaches agree on and what has been measured apart.

Evidence: insufficient that deloading is required. An international panel of strength and physique coaches calls deloading "ubiquitous yet under-researched", and says how to fit it into training for the best results is unknown. The authors also say it is unclear whether deloading is a necessary part of training to avoid the harmful effects of overtraining. What follows is expert opinion and practical experience, not trial results.
The panel's definition: "a period of reduced training stress designed to mitigate physiological and psychological fatigue, promote recovery, and enhance preparedness for subsequent training."
So you keep training, with less stress. Its purpose is to prepare you for what comes next. It does not build anything by itself. It is also different from a taper, which peaks you for a competition.

Claim: Reduces mental fatigue; Grade: Practical; Comment: A real, fair reason.. Claim: Needed to avoid overtraining; Grade: Insufficient; Comment: The authors leave this open.
That makes deloading low cost and low certainty. It is reasonable to adopt, as long as nobody claims more for it.

The paper's background reports that deloads are generally done every 4 to 6 weeks for about 7 days, ranging from one session to two weeks. That describes common practice, not a trial result. So this Handbook sets no required schedule.
Coaches on the panel agreed a deload could be planned in advance or decided by how you feel. The default here is the second: reduce when your own signals say so. Watch for a pattern:

Performance falling across several unrelated exercises for more than a week.. Normal warm-up loads feeling heavy.. Joint aches that outlast sessions and build week to week.. Trouble falling asleep, or waking early despite being tired.. Appetite and motivation both low for several days with no other reason.
One of these is noise. Several together, lasting, are a reason to reduce. If you prefer a planned lighter week, that is also fine.

The clearest point in that paper is universal agreement that training volume should come down, through fewer sets or repetitions. On intensity, the coaches accepted more than one approach: it could stay the same or drop.
So reduce volume first. Lowering the weight while keeping every set is unlikely to be the best version.

Most things called plateaus are not. Progress naturally slows as you train for longer, and it can look like a problem because your first months set an expectation that was never going to last.
Normal slowing needs patience. A true stall needs a diagnosis, and the answer is rarely the plan itself.

What you see: Same load on one exercise for a few weeks, repetitions rising; What it usually is: Progress. Double progression is working.. What you see: Slower than six months ago, still rising; What it usually is: Normal slowing. Not a plateau.. What you see: One exercise flat for several weeks, others rising; What it usually is: An exercise problem. You can diagnose it.. What you see: Most exercises flat or falling at once; What it usually is: A recovery problem. See Recovery and Deload week.
The key difference. A stall on one lift and a stall on most lifts are different problems. Treating them the same is why people add work when they should cut back.
You need a log to tell them apart. Without one, ordinary ups and downs look like a trend.
Start with the checks in Progressive overload: sleep, food, consistency, effort and fatigue. Three deserve extra attention:

Effort. Sets logged as hard that were not can cause a stall your log will not show.. Food. Body weight flat or falling while you are trying to gain muscle explains many stalls blamed on the plan.. Sleep. Sleep loss lowers performance, more so in afternoon and evening sessions. If your sleep was short in the weeks before a stall, take it seriously.
These causes are practical, not ranked by research. Work through them in this order:

Cause | What to do. Cause: The next weight step is too big; What to do: Common on small-muscle exercises. Add repetitions, or use smaller plates.. Cause: Your range has quietly shrunk; What to do: Load rose because the movement got smaller. Go back to full range at a lower load.. Cause: Another muscle gives out first; What to do: Grip on pulls, lower back on hinges, triceps on presses.. Cause: Your technique has drifted; What to do: Film a set and compare it with an older one.. Cause: The exercise does not suit you; What to do: The last resort. Swap with the test in Changing push exercises, and accept that your numbers reset.
Falling performance across several unrelated lifts points to recovery. Adding work is the wrong answer. Reduce volume first, then re-check after a week or two.
If that does not restore progress within a few weeks, look outside the gym: food, sleep, stress or health. See a clinician about lasting pain, nerve symptoms, or fatigue that survives real rest.
Once you have a diagnosis, the useful levers are the ones you already know. No special plateau technique is needed.

More weekly sets, if you have recovery to spare. Volume has the clearest link with growth, with returns that shrink. It is also the most expensive lever.. Truly hard sets, if you were stopping well short. Going all the way to failure has not been shown to add more.. Full range, if your range had shrunk.. More frequent sessions, mainly as a way to fit in your sets.. Time. Nobody wants this one, but progress is meant to slow.

Changing your whole plan is a weak fix. The instinct is to replace the plan. The ACSM found periodised programmes were not significantly better than non-periodised ones, and that many forms of training work. A new plan can feel like progress through novelty and soreness while resetting the numbers that would show if anything improved.

You will also see terms like minimum effective volume and maximum recoverable volume, presented as measurable numbers. They are useful as words for an idea: too little does little, and too much cannot be recovered from. It is not established that anyone can measure them for you, so this Handbook gives no numbers for them.

Acting on one bad session. Wait for a pattern.. Changing several things at once. You will not know what worked.. Adding work when performance is falling everywhere. It makes things worse.. Adding load at the cost of technique or range. Your log shows progress that did not happen.. Judging the plan on one stalled lift. Isolation exercises stall often and say little about the rest.. Comparing your pace with someone else's. Your history and circumstances differ.

Most plateaus are normal slowing.. One stalled exercise and many stalled exercises need opposite responses.. Rule out sleep, food, consistency and effort first.. If everything is falling, reduce. Do not add.. Replacing your whole plan is a weak fix, and it resets your numbers.
Nearly every gym habit gets defended on injury grounds, and many of those defences are untested. This chapter starts with the finding that has real evidence behind it.

Evidence: strong. Across six randomised trials with 7,738 people aged 12 to 40 and 177 injuries, strength training cut sports injury risk (relative risk 0.338, 0.238 to 0.480). Strength of evidence was rated high. A 10% rise in training volume cut injury risk by more than four percentage points.. Limits: the review covered sports injuries in athletic groups. It shows regular strength training is protective in those groups. It does not tell you how often a given gym exercise hurts people.

So the most supported protection is the training itself, progressed sensibly and kept up for years. Anything that keeps you training consistently helps. Anything that keeps interrupting training has a cost, including too much caution.

Claim | Grade | Comment. Claim: Strength training lowers injury risk; Grade: Strong, in sports groups; Comment: More training was linked with more protection.. Claim: Warming up prevents injury; Grade: Not settled; Comment: Warm up because it improves your session.. Claim: Stretching prevents injury; Grade: Not settled; Comment: Do not rely on it for protection.. Claim: Progressing gradually lowers risk; Grade: Practical; Comment: Fits the evidence above. Not tested alone here.. Claim: Good technique lowers risk; Grade: Practical; Comment: Hard to test and widely accepted.. Claim: Machines are safer than free weights; Grade: Insufficient; Comment: They differ in joint demand and stability, which affects your choice. That is not a safety ranking.
Most of what you control is here. It is practical guidance, not proven by a trial, but a sensible reason still counts for something.

Take the smallest step available. The percentage jump is what matters.. Do not raise load and volume in the same week. If something starts hurting, you will not know why.. Treat a return from a break as a return. Do not restart at the loads you left at.. Be patient with tendons. It is commonly explained that tendons adapt more slowly than muscle. No practical timeline is established, so treat this as a reason for patience, not a schedule.. Cut back when several exercises fall together. See Recovery and Deload week.
Good technique is widely accepted and hard to test directly. It stays a default because the reasoning is sound and following it costs nothing.

Load gained by shortening your range is not progress. See Building a leg session for when a partial is fair.. Stop a set when your technique changes. This is more useful than hitting a repetition number, and it avoids the open question of how close to failure to go.
Hard training is uncomfortable. Discomfort and pain are different things, and it is worth learning the difference early.

Expected | Stop and get it checked. Expected: Muscle fatigue and burning; Stop and get it checked: Sharp, stabbing or localised joint pain. Expected: Breathing hard; Stop and get it checked: Pain that worsens with each repetition. Expected: Soreness in the next days, especially after new work; Stop and get it checked: Pain at rest, or pain that wakes you at night. Expected: A movement feeling heavy; Stop and get it checked: Swelling, a joint giving way, or lost movement. Expected: Mild stiffness that eases as you warm up; Stop and get it checked: Numbness, tingling or weakness in a specific pattern
Anything in the right column means stop that exercise and find the cause. Training through it can turn a manageable problem into a long one.

Beyond a training adjustment. This Handbook does not diagnose. See a qualified clinician for:. Pain that is sharp, localised, present at rest, or wakes you at night.. Numbness, tingling or weakness in a specific pattern.. Swelling, a joint giving way, or sudden loss of range.. Any pain that has not improved after two weeks of truly reduced loading.. Fatigue or falling performance that continues after several weeks of reduced training.. Missed periods, frequent illness or bone pain alongside low food intake. These may point to low energy availability, a medical concern.. Distress about food, weight or missed sessions that affects daily life.. Getting checked early is not too cautious. It helps protect the consistency that matters most.

Did I do warm-up sets on my first heavy exercise?. Did those warm-up loads feel normal today?. Did I keep full range on every working set?. Did I stop each set when my technique changed?. Did I change only one thing this week?. Does anything match the right column above?

The best-supported protection is strength training itself, progressed sensibly and kept up.. Warm up for performance. Do not count on it to prevent injury.. It is not settled that stretching prevents injury.. Load management and technique are sensible defaults, not measured effects.. Learn the difference between discomfort and pain. The right column means stop.

Nutrition advice can make hundreds of decisions look equally important. They are not. A few things account for most of your result, and the rest only becomes worth your attention once those are handled.
This chapter sets out that order and the words the rest of this volume uses.
This order is practical guidance, built on the sources cited below.

Priority | What | Why it sits here. Priority: 1; What: Total energy; Why it sits here: Decides whether your weight goes up or down. Nothing below this overrides it.. Priority: 2; What: Total daily protein; Why it sits here: Helps decide how much of a weight change is muscle.. Priority: 3; What: Sticking with it; Why it sits here: A diet you abandon delivers nothing. Long-term success depends on it.. Priority: 4; What: Food quality, fibre, vitamins and minerals; Why it sits here: Matters for health, fullness and how you feel while training.. Priority: 5; What: Meal timing; Why it sits here: Real but small once the rows above are in place.. Priority: 6; What: Supplements; Why it sits here: Last, for a reason.

In practice. Many people turn this list upside down, worrying about supplements and meal timing while their total food and protein go unmeasured. If rows 1 and 2 are not handled, nothing below them will make up for it.
Calories are units of energy. Eating less than you use over time lowers your body mass. Eating more than you use raises it.

Goal | Energy position. Goal: Fat loss; Energy position: Eating below what you use, over time.. Goal: Staying the same; Energy position: Eating about what you use.. Goal: Muscle gain; Energy position: Eating a little above what you use, with enough protein and resistance training.

Evidence: strong. The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) states that fat loss is driven by a sustained calorie deficit, and that a wide range of diets, from low-fat to low-carbohydrate and ketogenic, can be similarly effective for body composition.. The same paper says the apparent advantage of low-carbohydrate and ketogenic diets comes from their higher protein content. Intermittent fasting showed no significant advantage over daily calorie restriction.. Its authors note a shortage of research in women and older people.
So use the eating pattern you can sustain. The pattern delivers the calories and protein. It does not do anything special by itself.

Nutrient | Energy | Main role here. Nutrient: Protein; Energy: About 4 kcal per gram; Main role here: Supplies amino acids for repair and building muscle.. Nutrient: Carbohydrate; Energy: About 4 kcal per gram; Main role here: A main fuel for repeated hard sets. Very low intake can show up as later sets fading.. Nutrient: Fat; Energy: About 9 kcal per gram; Main role here: Needed for absorbing some vitamins and for normal health. You need enough, not as much as possible.
A practical way to set your food: set protein first, because it has a clear target. Set fat next, at a level that keeps meals adequate and pleasant. Let carbohydrate fill the rest.

Carbohydrates are not the problem. Carbohydrate restriction has no shown advantage once calories and protein are matched. This matters in India: rice, roti, millets and dals are the affordable base of most meals. Cutting them out can hurt your training and make your diet harder to keep up.. The more useful question is how much total energy a meal gives you, and whether you are meeting your protein target.

Protein covers this properly. In brief: 1.4 to 2.0 g per kg of body weight a day is sufficient for most exercising people, and your daily total comes first. Common Indian sources include milk, curd, paneer, soya chunks, tofu, dals, rajma, chana, eggs where eaten, and whey where affordable.
The top three rows decide body composition. Row four decides how you feel on the way, and your health over decades. That is a different consideration, not a smaller one.

Fibre. WHO recommends adults get at least 25 g a day of naturally occurring fibre from food. Vegetables, fruit, pulses and whole grains supply it.. Fruit and vegetables. Eat a good range.. Highly processed foods. They are not forbidden. They are often high in calories and less filling, which can make a deficit harder to sustain. That is a practical argument, not a moral one.

Plant-based diets: nutrients that need attention. A well-planned vegetarian or vegan diet can support training. Some nutrients need attention, especially on a fully plant-based diet:. Vitamin B12. Not reliably available from plant foods. Vegans need fortified foods or a supplement.. Iron. Iron from plants is less well absorbed. A vitamin C source with the meal helps, and tea or coffee with the meal can reduce absorption.. Zinc. Absorption is lower from diets high in phytate, found in whole grains and pulses.. Omega-3. The body converts only a limited amount from plant sources.. Vitamin D. For most people this depends more on sun exposure than on food.. If you suspect a deficiency, get a blood test and have a clinician interpret it. Do not guess and self-prescribe.
Drink across the day, and expect to need more in hot weather or when you sweat heavily. Hydration and electrolytes covers this properly.

One meal does not undo your progress, and one meal does not create it. Your body responds to what you do most weeks, over months. This does not mean intake does not matter. It means choosing the right timescale, and it argues against the all-or-nothing pattern that ends many diets.

Get qualified support. This Handbook does not diagnose, prescribe clinical diets or interpret medical results. See a qualified clinician or dietitian if any of these apply:. A condition affected by diet, such as diabetes, kidney or liver disease, coeliac disease, thyroid disorders, PCOS or heart disease.. Pregnancy or breastfeeding.. A suspected deficiency, or abnormal blood results.. Unintended weight loss, missed periods, frequent illness or bone pain. These may point to low energy availability, a medical concern.. Distress about food, eating or body weight, restriction that feels hard to control, or eating that affects your daily life. Asking early is easier than asking late.

Total energy, total protein and sticking with it account for most of the outcome.. A wide range of diets can work. Choose the one you can sustain.. Carbohydrate restriction has no shown advantage once calories and protein are matched.. Set protein first, then enough fat, then carbohydrate with the rest.. Plant-based diets can work. B12, iron, zinc, omega-3 and vitamin D need attention.. Consistency over months beats precision on any one day.

You do not need to weigh every meal to eat well. A plate split into the right parts gets most meals close: half vegetables and fruit, a quarter grains, a quarter protein, a little healthy fat, and water to drink. The idea comes from Harvard's Healthy Eating Plate; the amounts below come from ICMR-NIN's guidelines for Indian diets.

One meal on the plate. Vegetables (more than fruit; potatoes do not count) · 0.4 · sabzi, salad, dal-vegetable mixes, greens. Fruit · 0.1 · whole fruit rather than juice. Grains, mostly whole · 0.25 · roti, brown or hand-pounded rice, millets, oats. Protein · 0.25 · dal, paneer, curd, eggs, chicken, fish, soya, chana
Add a small amount of healthy oil for cooking (groundnut, mustard, sesame, rice bran), and drink water, buttermilk, or tea and coffee with little or no sugar.

A day's food for about 2,000 kcal. Vegetables, including leafy greens · 400 · half the plate across the day [g or ml a day]. Cereals and millets (raw weight) · 250 · rice, wheat, millets [g or ml a day]. Milk and curd · 300 · ml [g or ml a day]. Fruit · 100 · one medium fruit [g or ml a day]. Pulses, eggs, meat or fish · 85 · raw weight; more for higher protein targets [g or ml a day]. Nuts and seeds · 35 · a small handful [g or ml a day]. Fats and oils · 27 · about 5 to 6 teaspoons, all cooking included [g or ml a day]

These are ICMR-NIN's amounts for a moderately active adult. Your Levlofit plan sets your own calories and protein, so your portions may be bigger or smaller; the shares stay similar. People who train hard usually need more protein than this day gives, which is why your plan adds protein foods. See Protein.

Common plate. Three rotis, a little sabzi, no protein. Big mound of rice, thin dal. Poha or upma alone for breakfast. Biryani with raita. Fruit juice with snacks. Better plate. Two rotis, a full bowl of dal or paneer sabzi, salad. Half the rice, a thick bowl of dal or rajma, a vegetable side. Poha with peanuts and a glass of milk or two eggs. Smaller biryani, a bigger raita, a salad, chicken or paneer pieces. Whole fruit, and water or buttermilk to drink

Simple rules that work. Build every main meal on the plate · Half vegetables and fruit, a quarter grains, a quarter protein.. Put protein in every meal · Dal, curd, paneer, eggs, chicken, fish or soya, every time.. Prefer whole foods · Whole grains, whole fruit, home-cooked over packaged most days.. Limit the extras, do not ban them · Sweets, fried snacks, sugary drinks and alcohol in small, planned amounts.. Keep snacking deliberate · If losing weight, snack only if it is planned in your day.

No single food makes or breaks a diet. "Superfoods" are marketing; what matters is the total over your days and weeks. A meal plan is good if it meets your calories and protein, has plenty of vegetables and fruit, and is one you will keep eating. See Nutrition fundamentals.

Diets you plan to "come off" usually end with the weight coming back. Change your normal meals a little at a time instead: one more vegetable, one more protein serving, one less sugary drink. Your favourite foods can stay; the portions and how often change. See Building habits that last.

At a restaurant, a canteen or a friend's house. Use your hand · A palm of protein, a fist of rice or grains, a cupped hand of snacks, a thumb of oil or ghee.. Compare to what you know · A restaurant curry bowl often holds 2 to 3 home servings, with more oil.. Log the closest match · Pick the nearest food in the diary; close is better than skipping.. Learn from repeats · Weigh a home serving of foods you eat often once, so your eye learns.
See Eating out, travel and occasions.

Half vegetables and fruit, a quarter grains, a quarter protein, a little healthy oil, water to drink.. ICMR's day for 2,000 kcal: 400 g vegetables, 250 g cereals, 300 ml milk, 100 g fruit, 85 g pulses or meat, 35 g nuts, 27 g oil.. Protein in every meal, extras planned not banned, and changes you can keep.
Protein is the one macronutrient with a clear daily number to aim for, which is why it gets a chapter of its own. It supplies the amino acids your body uses to repair and build muscle.
Protein does not build muscle on its own. Training asks your body to adapt, and protein is part of what pays for it.

Evidence: position stand. The International Society of Sports Nutrition states that 1.4 to 2.0 g of protein per kg of body weight per day is sufficient for most exercising people for building and keeping muscle.. The same paper calls the evidence for intakes above 3.0 g per kg novel. It may help body composition in resistance-trained people, but it is not established.

Situation | Daily intake | Standing. Situation: Healthy, inactive Indian adult; Daily intake: 0.83 g per kg; Standing: The Indian RDA. It covers daily needs, not training.. Situation: Training, building or keeping muscle; Daily intake: 1.4 to 2.0 g per kg; Standing: Position stand.. Situation: Already lean, resistance training, eating below your needs; Daily intake: 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of fat-free mass; Standing: "May be required", so not a firm rule. Fat-free mass is a smaller number than body weight.
These figures are per kg of body weight, except the last row. If you train and eat between about 1.4 and 2.0 g per kg, you are in the supported range.
Your total for the day comes first. How you spread it is a smaller refinement.

Question | What the position stand says. Question: How much per meal?; What the position stand says: About 0.25 g per kg of body weight, or 20 to 40 g. It says the findings are mixed and depend on age and recent training.. Question: How often?; What the position stand says: Ideally spread evenly, every 3 to 4 hours.. Question: What makes a dose work?; What the position stand says: All the essential amino acids, with 700 to 3000 mg of leucine.. Question: Before sleep?; What the position stand says: 30 to 40 g of casein raises overnight muscle protein synthesis.
For most people this comes down to one habit: have a real protein source at each main meal instead of eating most of it at dinner. That helps both your daily total and how it is spread.
You do not have to drink protein within minutes of finishing a workout.

Evidence: position stand. The best time is likely a matter of what you tolerate, since benefits come from eating before or after training. The effect of exercise lasts at least 24 hours, though it likely fades with time.
In practice. Eat a meal with protein within a few hours before or after training, then stop thinking about it.

Proteins that digest quickly and are high in essential amino acids and leucine stimulate muscle protein synthesis most. The position stand suggests focusing on whole foods that contain all the essential amino acids.

Food, raw | Protein. Food, raw: Soya chunks, 50 g dry; Protein: 25.7 g. Food, raw: Paneer, 100 g; Protein: 18.9 g. Food, raw: Chicken breast, skinless, 100 g; Protein: 21.8 g. Food, raw: Masoor dal, 50 g dry; Protein: 12.2 g. Food, raw: Kala chana, 50 g dry; Protein: 9.4 g. Food, raw: Whole egg, 50 g without shell; Protein: 6.6 g. Food, raw: Cow milk, 250 g; Protein: 8.2 g
These are for planning. Where a pack has a label, trust the label.

The position stand says research on plant proteins such as pea, rice and hemp is limited. In one study it reports, protein synthesis after resistance exercise was about 31% higher with whey than with soy. In another, 48 g a day of whey or rice protein gave similar gains over 8 weeks in experienced lifters.

Claim | Standing. Claim: "Only animal protein builds muscle."; Standing: Not supported. Rice protein matched whey in the 8-week study above, though the research is limited.. Claim: "More protein is always better."; Standing: Not shown. 1.4 to 2.0 g per kg is sufficient for most exercising people, and the evidence above 3.0 g per kg is still novel.. Claim: "You need a shake straight after training."; Standing: False. The effect of exercise lasts at least 24 hours.. Claim: "Protein powder is necessary."; Standing: False. The position stand calls it a practical option, and says daily needs can be met from whole foods.
If you have kidney disease. Your doctor should set your protein intake. Levlofit does not advise on it.

Your Levlofit plan sets a daily target. Judge it across the week, not one day at a time.. Build each main meal around a protein source.. If you are often short, add curd or milk at breakfast, dal or soya at one main meal, and eggs if you eat them.. Use powder if it makes the target easier to reach. It is not a better food.

1.4 to 2.0 g per kg a day is sufficient for most exercising people.. Lean people training on fewer calories may need more, counted per kg of fat-free mass.. Your daily total matters most. Spreading it out is a smaller refinement.. There is no narrow window after training. The effect lasts at least a day.
Vegetarian and vegan diets can support muscle gain when protein is planned carefully: protein-dense foods at every meal and a mix of sources. Direct evidence in vegan diets is limited.
Dry soya chunks are the richest common vegetarian source, at about 51.5 g of protein in 100 g. This value is from a close match, defatted soy flour.

Food, per 100 g raw | Protein | Energy. Food, per 100 g raw: Masoor dal; Protein: 24.4 g; Energy: 322 kcal. Food, per 100 g raw: Moong dal; Protein: 23.9 g; Energy: 326 kcal. Food, per 100 g raw: Peanuts; Protein: 23.7 g; Energy: 520 kcal. Food, per 100 g raw: Chana dal; Protein: 21.6 g; Energy: 329 kcal. Food, per 100 g raw: Paneer; Protein: 18.9 g; Energy: 258 kcal
These values are from the Indian Food Composition Tables.

Meal | Options. Meal: Breakfast; Options: Moong chilla or besan cheela, or poha with peanuts and curd. Meal: Lunch; Options: Dal plus rajma or chana with roti; pulses and grains cover each other's gaps. Meal: Snack; Options: Roasted chana, sprouts chaat or a glass of milk. Meal: Dinner; Options: Soya chunk curry, paneer bhurji or tofu with vegetables
Vegetarian | Vegan. Vegetarian: Paneer, curd and milk; Vegan: Tofu and soya chunks. Vegetarian: Dals, chana and rajma; Vegan: Dals, chana, rajma and sprouts. Vegetarian: Soya chunks; Vegan: Peanuts
Levlofit rule. If you eat vegan, aim for the upper end of your protein range. This is a Levlofit rule, not a research finding.
Evidence: strong. Soy did not change male hormones across clinical studies, at any dose tested.

Vegetarian and vegan diets can support muscle gain when protein is planned carefully. Direct evidence in vegan diets is limited.. Soya chunks, dals, peanuts and paneer are dense sources.. Mix pulses and grains through the day.

Body composition is the balance of muscle and fat in your body. It changes for two reasons: your training, and your energy intake. This chapter covers choosing a direction, setting a pace, estimating your starting point, and measuring the result well enough to know if it is working.

Goal | Energy position | What decides success. Goal: Fat loss; Energy position: Sustained deficit; What decides success: Enough protein and continued training, so you lose mostly fat.. Goal: Staying the same; Energy position: About balanced; What decides success: An underrated choice. Strength can still improve at a stable weight.. Goal: Muscle gain; Energy position: Small surplus; What decides success: Keep it small. In practice, a big surplus mostly adds fat, because muscle grows slowly.
These are reasonable defaults, not research findings:

If you | Reasonable default. If you: Are new to resistance training; Reasonable default: Train and eat enough protein at about maintenance. Gaining muscle and losing fat together is most likely here.. If you: Carry noticeable extra fat; Reasonable default: Lose fat first. The ISSN says a larger deficit is more suitable at higher body fat.. If you: Are lean and want more muscle; Reasonable default: A small surplus.. If you: Are unsure; Reasonable default: Maintenance, with attention to protein and training. It gives you time to decide.

Every calorie estimate is a guess with a range. Calculators give one confident number for your daily needs. Levlofit starts from an equation too. Individuals vary around any such estimate, and activity levels add more uncertainty. Treat the number as a starting guess, not a measurement.
Your own trend is more reliable. It takes two to three weeks:

Eat in a fairly consistent way and log it.. Weigh yourself in the same conditions most days: after waking, after using the toilet, before eating.. Compare one week's average with the next. A stable average means you are near maintenance, whatever the calculator said.. Adjust from there.

Daily body weight can swing by a kilogram or more from water, food in your gut, salt, carbohydrate and, for many women, the menstrual cycle. These swings are often larger than a week's real change, so one weigh-in tells you little.
The rule to use. Judge your weight by a seven-day average, not a single reading. Average the last seven mornings and compare that week to week.
Weight also cannot separate muscle from fat. Track it along with your lifts, measurements, photos in consistent conditions, and how your clothes fit.
Use a percentage of your body weight, because the same kilograms mean very different things at different sizes.

Goal | Pace | How firm this is. Goal: Fat loss; Pace: About 0.5 to 1% of body weight a week, slower as you get leaner; How firm this is: Moderate. One review found this pace may be better for keeping lean mass in lean, resistance-trained people.. Goal: Muscle gain; Pace: Slow enough that weight rises over months, not weeks; How firm this is: No precise figure is established.

Evidence: moderate. Slower weight loss can better preserve lean mass in leaner people, and a larger deficit may suit those with higher body fat. Long-term success depends on sticking with it, which is another reason to avoid extreme deficits. Research in women and older people is limited.
This is often called recomposition. It is real, and practical experience suggests it is more likely in certain situations:
You are new to resistance training.. You are returning after a long break.. You carry more body fat.. Your protein is adequate and your training is consistent. These are requirements, not boosters.
No reliable rate is established. As you train for longer, it usually gets slower and harder, and working on one goal at a time may become simpler.

Spot reduction. Training one body part is a poor way to lose fat from that area. Ab work builds your abs, but expect the fat over them to change as your overall body fat changes. Where you lose fat first is largely outside your control.
Use these practical responses after two to three weeks of data:

What you see | Reasonable response. What you see: Average flat, goal is fat loss; Reasonable response: Eat a little less or move a little more. Change one thing.. What you see: Average falling faster than you intended; Reasonable response: Add some food back. Faster is not better.. What you see: Average climbing quickly while gaining; Reasonable response: Reduce the surplus.. What you see: Performance dropping across several exercises; Reasonable response: Check sleep and total food before changing your plan.. What you see: Energy, mood or appetite staying low; Reasonable response: Your deficit may be too large or have run too long.
Adjust on trends, and change one thing at a time. Changing every week is usually too often to tell what worked.

Low energy availability and disordered eating. Long or severe calorie restriction carries risks beyond your training plan. See a qualified clinician if you have:. Missed or irregular periods.. Frequent illness, lasting fatigue or repeated bone injuries.. Low sex drive, disturbed sleep or often feeling cold.. Distress about food or weight, restriction that feels hard to control, or eating that affects your daily life.. These are medical concerns. Asking for help early is easier than asking later.

Treating a calculator as a measurement. It is a starting guess.. Judging progress on one weigh-in. Daily swings often exceed weekly change.. Cutting too hard. It can cost muscle, training quality and your ability to keep going.. Bulking hard. Much of the excess is likely to be fat.. Adjusting every few days. That is too soon to separate signal from noise.. Letting protein drop in a deficit. It matters most when food is lowest.

Pick a direction and hold it long enough to judge. Maintenance is a fair choice.. Calorie calculators are guesses. Your two-week trend is the measurement.. Judge weight by a seven-day average.. For fat loss, about 0.5 to 1% of body weight a week is a reasonable pace.. Gaining muscle while losing fat can happen, with no reliable rate.. You cannot choose where you lose fat.

passages.chapterTitle: Losing and gaining weight: your questions
passages.text: Weight change follows one rule: eat less energy than you use and you lose weight; eat more and you gain. Every diet that works does it by changing that balance. The hard part is that both sides of the balance are only estimates, so the scale over weeks is your real measure.

passages.chapterTitle: Losing and gaining weight: your questions
passages.text: Why people do not lose. They eat more than they think: oil, drinks, snacks, sauces and weekends add up. Their energy use is lower than the calculator said. Calories "burned" by a watch were eaten back. Why people do not gain. They eat less than they think: small breakfasts, skipped meals, busy days. Their energy use is higher than the calculator said. Extra activity was not covered with extra food

passages.chapterTitle: Losing and gaining weight: your questions
passages.text: In a classic study, people who said they could not lose weight on very little food were eating about twice what they reported and moving less than they reported. This is normal human error, not dishonesty. The fix is the same both ways: track honestly for two to three weeks and adjust by the trend.

passages.chapterTitle: Losing and gaining weight: your questions
passages.text: Finding the number that works for you. Start with an estimate · Your Levlofit plan already gives one; any calculator is only a starting point.. Adjust by goal · About 10 to 20% below maintenance to lose, 10 to 20% above to gain.. Weigh in regularly · Same time, same conditions: morning, after the toilet, before food.. Read the trend · Compare weekly averages, not single days. Daily weight can swing by 1 to 2 kg from water, salt, food and glycogen.. Adjust after 2 to 3 weeks · No change in the trend: move calories 100 to 200 a day in the direction you need.. Repeat as you change · Your energy use falls as you lose weight and rises as you gain, so targets need updating.

passages.chapterTitle: Losing and gaining weight: your questions
passages.text: See Calories and body composition and Body weight tracking.

passages.chapterTitle: Losing and gaining weight: your questions
passages.text: Which comes first. Clearly carrying extra fat? · Lose weight first, and lift to keep your muscle. · Go on to the next question.. Clearly thin? · Gain weight with lifting; some fat gain is expected and fine. · Go on to the next question.. Normal weight but soft and not strong ("skinny fat")? · Build muscle at a small surplus, or at maintenance as a beginner; choose the phase you mind less. · Lean enough but not big enough: gain. Big enough but not lean enough: lose.

passages.chapterTitle: Losing and gaining weight: your questions
passages.text: If your goal is performance, avoid hard cuts. Neither choice is permanent: you can gain then lose, or lose then gain. Long-term body change asks you to accept a few months of looking a little fatter or a little smaller than you would like.

passages.chapterTitle: Losing and gaining weight: your questions
passages.text: It happens most in beginners, people returning after a break, and people carrying more fat. Lean, experienced lifters rarely manage both. Losing slowly helps: athletes who lost about 0.7% of body weight a week gained muscle, while those losing about 1.4% a week did not.

passages.chapterTitle: Losing and gaining weight: your questions
passages.text: Weekly weight loss and keeping muscle. 0 · 0.5 · Slow: easiest to keep or even gain muscle [% of body weight a week]. 0.5 · 1 · Steady: the usual target; keep lifting and eat enough protein [% of body weight a week]. 1 · 1.5 · Fast: more muscle at risk; fine for short phases with extra fat to lose [% of body weight a week]. 1.5 · 3 · Very fast: muscle loss, hunger and rebound more likely [% of body weight a week]

passages.chapterTitle: Losing and gaining weight: your questions
passages.text: Recomposition is slower and harder to track, because the scale may not move. If the scale is not moving and you are not sure it is working, pick one direction for a few months.

passages.chapterTitle: Losing and gaining weight: your questions
passages.text: Common belief. My metabolism is unusually slow or fast. Eating too little puts me in starvation mode and stops weight loss. Ectomorphs, mesomorphs and endomorphs need different diets. I am a hard gainer. What the research shows. Most of the difference in resting energy use between people is explained by body size and muscle; true outliers are rare and medical.. Energy use falls somewhat as you lose weight, but a moderate deficit still works; weight loss does not stop while you truly eat less.. Body types come from a 1940s theory about personality; they do not predict how you gain or lose. Everyone follows the same energy balance.. Hard gainers who eat more, gain. Some people need far more food than they expect.

passages.chapterTitle: Losing and gaining weight: your questions
passages.text: If you truly eat less over months and the scale does not move, or eat much more and still do not gain, see a doctor: a thyroid or other medical problem is then possible.

passages.chapterTitle: Losing and gaining weight: your questions
passages.text: Home body-fat scales and handheld devices use electrical impedance, which shifts with water, food and time of day; readings are often off by several percent and not even consistently off. Use body weight, a waist measurement and photos instead. If your weight is falling, you are losing fat. See Body measurements and Progress photos.

passages.chapterTitle: Losing and gaining weight: your questions
passages.text: Lifting while you lose weight keeps your muscle, so more of what you lose is fat and you look better at the end. Hunger is normal in a deficit; protein, vegetables, fibre and enough sleep help. Plan a few weeks at maintenance after 8 to 12 weeks of losing, to rest from dieting. See Body fat and getting lean.

passages.chapterTitle: Losing and gaining weight: your questions
passages.text: If the scale is not going up, you are not eating enough yet, whatever the plan says. Add 200 to 300 kcal a day and check again in two weeks. Easy extras: milk, curd, peanuts and peanut butter, bananas, an extra roti, ghee on dal, a shake. See Gaining muscle and weight.

passages.chapterTitle: Losing and gaining weight: your questions
passages.text: For weight, calories come first; diets with very different carbs and fat lose the same weight when calories and protein are matched. For body composition, protein comes next; carbs and fat then fill the rest of your calories in whatever mix you enjoy. Keep at least some fat (about 0.6 g per kg body weight is a common floor) for health.

passages.chapterTitle: Losing and gaining weight: your questions
passages.text: Calories decide weight; both sides of the balance are estimates, so trust your weekly average weight.. Change calories by 10 to 20% for your goal and adjust every 2 to 3 weeks.. Bulk or cut by what you mind less; aim to lose about 0.5 to 1% of body weight a week.. Slow metabolism, starvation mode and body types explain very little; consistent eating explains most.. Ignore body-fat scales; use weight, waist and photos.
Muscle is built slowly. A small surplus plus hard training adds muscle; a big surplus mostly adds fat.
For beginners and intermediates, as a share of body weight each week:
Weekly gain | What it means. Weekly gain: Up to 0.25%; What it means: Slow and lean. Weekly gain: 0.25% to 0.5%; What it means: Target pace. Weekly gain: 0.5% to 1%; What it means: Mostly fat
Aim for a surplus of 10 to 20% above maintenance. Levlofit starts at 10%.
Evidence: strong. In a meta-analysis of 49 trials, protein beyond about 1.6 g per kg a day gave no further average gain in muscle from training.
See Protein for the full picture.

Add a meal. Milk and a banana, or curd and poha, between meals.. Use dense foods. Peanuts, a little ghee on roti, paneer, dry fruits.. Drink some calories. Milk, lassi or a banana shake.. Weigh weekly. Levlofit rule: if the trend is off pace for 3 weeks, adjust by 150 to 200 kcal a day.

Lean gain | Dirty bulk. Lean gain: Small surplus, weight up slowly; Dirty bulk: Eating everything in sight. Lean gain: Hard training 3 to 5 days a week; Dirty bulk: Gaining over 1% a week. Lean gain: Advanced lifters: aim for the lower end; Dirty bulk: Long fat-loss diet needed afterwards
A small surplus, about 10% above maintenance, adds muscle with less fat.. Protein beyond about 1.6 g per kg gave no extra average muscle gain.. A big surplus mostly adds fat.
Eating too little for too long costs muscle, energy and health. Levlofit never sets your calories below your resting burn, but you are the first to notice when eating has become a struggle.

Your resting burn (BMR) is the floor. Levlofit never sets your calorie target below it.. No deficit when underweight. When your BMI is below the healthy range, Levlofit keeps you at maintenance instead.

Signs to slow down the diet | Signs to talk to a doctor. Signs to slow down the diet: Weight falling faster than your planned pace for two weeks or more; Signs to talk to a doctor: Periods stopping or becoming irregular. Signs to slow down the diet: Strength dropping for several weeks in a row; Signs to talk to a doctor: Fainting or dizziness. Signs to slow down the diet: Constant hunger, poor sleep or low energy; Signs to talk to a doctor: Feeling unable to stop restricting food, bingeing, making yourself sick, or exercising to make up for eating. Signs to slow down the diet: ; Signs to talk to a doctor: Thoughts about food, weight or your body taking over most of the day
Evidence: moderate. In lean athletes, low energy availability is linked to lower testosterone in men and is the proposed cause of missed periods, called athletic amenorrhea, in women.

Question | If yes | If no. Question: Is your BMI below the healthy range?; If yes: Do not diet. Levlofit keeps you at maintenance and builds strength instead.; If no: Go to the next question.. Question: Does any sign in the doctor list apply to you?; If yes: Pause the fat-loss phase and talk to a doctor.; If no: Carry on at the planned pace and review every 2 to 3 weeks.

Getting help. This chapter cannot diagnose anything. Eating disorders are medical conditions that need care from a doctor or specialist.. If you feel overwhelmed, call Tele-MANAS on 14416, free and confidential.

Levlofit never sets calories below your BMR, and keeps underweight users at maintenance.. Slow the diet if weight falls faster than planned or strength keeps dropping.. Missed periods, fainting or a loss of control around food mean talk to a doctor.
Meal timing is oversold, though it is not nothing either. It helps in some situations. Those situations are narrower than the marketing claims, and wider than "it does not matter".

What | Effect | Grade. What: Total daily energy; Effect: Decides whether weight goes up or down; Grade: Strong. What: Total daily protein; Effect: Helps decide how much of the change is muscle; Grade: Strong. What: Spreading protein across the day; Effect: Real, but secondary. Every 3 to 4 hours is the stated ideal; Grade: Moderate. What: Eating around training; Effect: Can support performance and recovery; Grade: Moderate. What: Carbohydrate timing; Effect: Matters when you need rapid recovery. Otherwise much less important; Grade: Moderate. What: Number of meals; Effect: Limited effect on weight loss and body composition when not exercising; can help appetite; Grade: Moderate. What: Timing to the minute; Effect: None shown; Grade: Insufficient
The claim is that you must have protein within about 30 minutes of training or the session is wasted. The position stands do not support that.

Evidence: moderate. The ISSN protein paper says the best time is likely a matter of what you tolerate, since benefits come from eating before or after training. The effect of exercise lasts at least 24 hours, though it likely fades with time.. The ISSN timing paper says protein within two hours after exercise strongly stimulates muscle protein synthesis, and that the size and timing of your meal before training affects how much post-training protein matters.
So think in hours, not minutes, and remember the meal before training counts as well.
The goal is to feel fuelled and comfortable. Two patterns work:

A normal meal a few hours before. Protein and carbohydrate, with moderate fat and fibre so you are comfortable when you start.. A lighter snack closer to training. Mostly carbohydrate, with some protein, and low in fat and fibre.
Indian options include curd with fruit, poha or upma, oats with milk, a banana with milk, rice with dal, toast with peanut butter, and roti with paneer.
No exact timing is established. What feels comfortable varies with the person and the meal, so try it and see.

Training without food is a scheduling choice. In practice it suits some people and not others. If eating first makes you uncomfortable, train and eat afterwards. If you feel weak or light-headed, eat something small first. If that continues, or if you have diabetes or another medical condition, ask your doctor.
Have a meal with protein and carbohydrate within the next few hours. That is the whole recommendation.
You do not need a shake before leaving the gym. It is also fine if that is the easiest way to reach your daily protein.

When carbohydrate timing really matters. Fast glycogen refuelling plans are for when you need rapid recovery, such as training twice in one day or competing on back-to-back days.. The ISSN paper says that outside such situations, when daily carbohydrate matches your needs, the importance of timed carbohydrate is "notably decreased".. If you train once a day, eat enough carbohydrate across the day and leave it there.

The number of meals is largely a practical choice. Changing meal frequency has shown limited effect on weight loss and body composition when not exercising, with stronger evidence for appetite and fullness.

Pattern | Suits. Pattern: Three main meals; Suits: Most people. Fits typical Indian eating.. Pattern: Three meals plus one or two protein snacks; Suits: Anyone struggling to reach a protein target.. Pattern: Fewer, larger meals; Suits: People who like big meals, or whose schedule prevents regular eating. Protein takes more planning.. Pattern: More, smaller meals; Suits: People who need a lot of food and find big meals uncomfortable.
The ISSN suggests spreading protein every 3 to 4 hours, which suits three meals plus a snack. If your plan includes pre- and post-workout meals, they count towards this.

Skipping meals to save calories, then overeating later. This is really a total-food problem.. Training after a long gap without food, then blaming the plan. Food belongs on your stall checklist.. Eating a large, fatty, high-fibre meal right before training. It can be uncomfortable.. Trying new food on a day that matters. Test it on an ordinary day first.. Perfecting your timing while your daily total goes unmeasured. Fix the big things first.. Treating a post-workout shake as a requirement. It is a convenience.

The effect of training lasts at least a day. Think in hours, not minutes.. Total energy and protein come first. Timing is a refinement.. Spreading protein every 3 to 4 hours is the stated ideal.. Fast carbohydrate plans are for rapid recovery, not ordinary training.. Meal frequency is a practical choice.. Training without eating first is a scheduling choice.
A small budget changes which foods you use, not what your body needs. Total energy, protein and sticking with it still decide your result.

Practical guidance. Prices and availability vary by city, season and household, so most of this chapter is practical advice rather than research. The protein figures come from food composition tables.
When money is tight, compare cost per gram of protein, not price per kilogram. Protein is usually the expensive part of your food, and carbohydrate is usually cheap.

Work it out once. Divide the pack price by the grams of protein in the pack. Do this for the five or six sources you can actually buy. You only need to do it occasionally, and the cheapest food by weight is often not the cheapest protein.

Dry soya chunks and pulses often work out cheap per gram of protein, dairy often sits in the middle, and paneer, whey and meat are often more expensive. Check your own local prices, since this is a starting guess.

Food, raw | Protein | Role on a tight budget. Food, raw: Soya chunks, 50 g dry; Protein: 25.7 g; Role on a tight budget: The workhorse. High in protein and keeps well. This value is from a close match, defatted soy flour.. Food, raw: Masoor dal, 50 g dry; Protein: 12.2 g; Role on a tight budget: Cheap and already in many meals. Count it towards your target.. Food, raw: Rajma, 50 g dry; Protein: 10 g; Role on a tight budget: Also gives fibre. Dry is usually cheaper than tinned.. Food, raw: Kala chana, 50 g dry; Protein: 9.4 g; Role on a tight budget: Also gives fibre, and keeps well.. Food, raw: Cow milk, 250 g; Protein: 8.2 g; Role on a tight budget: Easy to add across the day with no preparation.. Food, raw: Whole egg, 50 g without shell; Protein: 6.6 g; Role on a tight budget: If you eat them, they need little preparation.. Food, raw: Paneer, 100 g; Protein: 18.9 g; Role on a tight budget: Dense in protein, but often costs more per gram.. Food, raw: Peanuts, 50 g; Protein: 11.8 g; Role on a tight budget: Useful, but high in calories. Count them if you are in a deficit.. Food, raw: Whey powder, one scoop; Protein: Check the label; Role on a tight budget: Convenient, not necessary. Compare its cost per gram of protein first.
These are for planning. Where a pack has a label, trust the label. Curd is useful too, and it can cost less set at home from milk. Check the label on packaged curd for its protein.

Rice, atta, oats, potatoes, bananas, and seasonal fruit and vegetables are usually inexpensive. For fat, peanuts, seeds and ordinary cooking oil do the job. If you have money left over, a wider range of vegetables and enough fruit will make your food more pleasant, and healthier.

Meal | Example | What it adds. Meal: Breakfast; Example: Oats cooked in milk, with a banana; What it adds: Protein from milk, carbohydrate, little skill needed. Meal: Lunch; Example: Rice, dal, a vegetable, curd; What it adds: A standard meal, often close already. A larger serving of dal is an easy upgrade.. Meal: Snack; Example: Peanuts, curd or an egg; What it adds: Cheap protein when you might otherwise skip it. Meal: Dinner; Example: Soya chunk curry with rice or roti, plus a vegetable; What it adds: A big, low-cost protein serving
Notice this is not a special diet. It is an ordinary Indian day with the protein parts made bigger. That is often the cheapest way to your target, and the easiest to keep up.
Hostel, shared kitchen, no time or no skill? These still work:

Milk and curd, with no preparation.. Sattu mixed into water or milk.. Roasted chana, which keeps well and travels easily.. Peanuts.. Boiled eggs, if you can boil water.. Oats soaked overnight in milk with fruit.. Whey, if its cost per gram of protein works for you.
If your meals come from a mess or canteen, add to what is served: extra dal or curd at the meal, and a protein snack in your room. You can tell Levlofit about mess meals in your diet settings.

Buy dry staples in bulk if you can store them. Rice, dal, soya chunks and oats keep well.. Buy seasonal produce. It is usually cheaper.. Cook once, eat several times. Batch cooking dal or chana saves fuel and time.. Carry water. Sugary drinks cost money and add calories without much fullness.. Make curd or paneer at home if you can.. Compare supplements with food before you buy.

Batch cooking and food safety. Batch cooking is a main budget strategy, but it can be risky if handled carelessly, particularly with cooked rice and pulses in hot weather.. Cool cooked food quickly, refrigerate it promptly and reheat it thoroughly. Do not keep leftovers at room temperature for long. If your fridge is unreliable, cook smaller amounts more often.

Assuming eating well must be expensive. Soya chunks, dal, eggs and milk can be affordable.. Buying supplements before food. Food often gives you more protein for the money.. Skipping meals to save money. It cuts energy, and can lead to overeating later.. Paying for "fitness" branded food. Compare its protein and price with ordinary food.. Forgetting to count dal. Protein already in your meals counts.. Cutting protein first. It is the part most likely to go when money is short, and one that matters most.

Your targets do not change with your budget. Your foods do.. Compare cost per gram of protein.. Soya chunks, dal, chana, milk, curd and eggs can carry most of the load.. The cheapest plan is usually an ordinary Indian day with bigger protein servings.. No-cook options work: sattu, curd, roasted chana, peanuts and soaked oats.. Take care with cooked rice and pulses in warm weather.

Supplements come last in the order of importance, behind energy, protein, sticking with it, food quality and timing. For most people, the list worth buying is very short. It is not empty, though. Two have position stands behind them.
Ask yourself four questions. If any answer is no, your money is probably better spent elsewhere.
Am I training consistently, and progressing on something?. Am I reaching my protein target most days?. Does my total food match my goal?. Am I sleeping enough, and regularly?

Evidence: strong. The ISSN calls creatine monohydrate "the most effective ergogenic nutritional supplement currently available to athletes" for increasing high-intensity exercise capacity and lean body mass during training.. Dose: once muscles are saturated, 3 to 5 g a day generally maintains stores. Some studies suggest larger athletes may need 5 to 10 g a day. The fastest way to raise stores is 5 g four times a day for 5 to 7 days, but you do not have to do this.. Safety: the paper reports that short and long-term use, up to 30 g a day for 5 years, is safe and well tolerated in healthy people. It also reports that creatine either has no effect on or reduces injury, dehydration and cramping in athletes.
What follows in practice:

Buy monohydrate. It is the form the ISSN paper is about, and usually a low-cost one.. Take it daily at any time you will remember. Stores build over time, so exact timing matters little.. Expect a small weight gain at first. Creatine holds a little water. Your seven-day average may step up.

The safety statement has a limit. That safety evidence is for healthy people. If you have kidney disease, any other diagnosed condition, or take prescription medicine, ask a clinician first. Levlofit does not advise on supplements alongside disease.

Evidence: strong for endurance, moderate for strength. The ISSN says caffeine "has been shown to acutely enhance various aspects of exercise performance in many but not all studies". Aerobic endurance shows the most consistent moderate to large benefit. Benefits for strength and muscular endurance are small to moderate.. Dose: 3 to 6 mg per kg of body weight has consistently improved performance. The minimum may be as low as 2 mg per kg. Very high doses, such as 9 mg per kg, bring more side effects and do not seem to be needed.. Timing: most commonly about 60 minutes before exercise.. Differences between people: genes and your usual caffeine intake may change how you respond, including effects on sleep and anxiety.
Caffeine and sleep. Sleep loss lowers performance. A dose before training that costs you sleep is a poor trade, so if you train in the evening, try less caffeine or none.
Coffee and tea contain caffeine, so you do not need a pre-workout product to get it. Blends that hide their doses cannot be judged.

This is food in a convenient form. The ISSN calls it a practical way to get enough protein, while noting you can meet your needs from whole foods. Buy it if it makes your target easier to reach, and compare its cost per gram of protein with food first.
These are general notes, not advice for you personally.

Supplement | When it makes sense | Note. Supplement: Vitamin B12; When it makes sense: Needed on a fully plant-based diet.; Note: No expected benefit if your levels are already fine.. Supplement: Vitamin D; When it makes sense: When sun exposure is limited or your levels are low.; Note: Correcting a deficiency makes sense. Taking excess does not.. Supplement: Iron; When it makes sense: Only for a confirmed deficiency.; Note: Do not self-prescribe. Too much iron is harmful. Get a blood test and see a clinician.. Supplement: Omega-3; When it makes sense: When you eat little long-chain omega-3, particularly on plant-based diets.; Note: Not a performance supplement.. Supplement: Multivitamin; When it makes sense: As low-cost cover for a narrow diet.; Note: It does not replace food.

Blood results. Levlofit does not interpret blood results. The right order is a test, then a clinician's reading, then a dose if you need one. This matters even more during pregnancy or breastfeeding, with any diagnosed condition, or with prescription medicine.
These are the official reference intakes and upper limits for healthy adults, not doses for you. Levlofit's Supplement guide and Diet tab tie each one to a meal.

Supplement | Best time | Reference intake (adults) | Upper limit. Supplement: Vitamin D3; Best time: With a main meal that has some fat; Reference intake (adults): 600 IU (15 mcg) a day; Upper limit: 4,000 IU (100 mcg) a day unless a doctor prescribes more. Supplement: Vitamin B12; Best time: Once a day, any time; Reference intake (adults): 2.5 mcg a day; Upper limit: None set; tablets often carry far more because little is absorbed. Supplement: Omega-3 (EPA plus DHA); Best time: With a meal, to absorb it and avoid fishy burps; Reference intake (adults): No Indian reference intake; capsules give 250 to 1,000 mg; Upper limit: Up to 5 g a day from supplements is considered safe. Supplement: Iron; Best time: Empty stomach, with vitamin C; 2 hours from tea, coffee, milk and calcium; Reference intake (adults): 19 mg (men), 29 mg (women) a day; Upper limit: 45 mg a day without medical advice. Supplement: Magnesium; Best time: With dinner; Reference intake (adults): 400 to 420 mg (men), 310 to 320 mg (women) from all food; Upper limit: 350 mg a day from supplements. Supplement: Calcium; Best time: With meals, no more than 500 mg at once; Reference intake (adults): 1,000 mg a day; Upper limit: 2,500 mg a day from food and supplements. Supplement: Creatine monohydrate; Best time: Any time, every day; Reference intake (adults): 3 to 5 g a day; Upper limit: Not set; long-term use at these doses is safe in healthy people

Keep these apart. Iron and calcium · At least 2 hours apart; calcium blocks iron absorption.. Iron and tea or coffee · 2 hours apart; tannins block iron.. Zinc and iron · Separate high doses; they compete for absorption.. Caffeine and sleep · None within about 6 hours of bed.
These have no strong case behind them in this Handbook's sources. That is not proof they can never work, but the burden of proof sits with the product.

Product | Why not. Product: Testosterone boosters; Why not: No strong reason to expect a meaningful change in your body composition.. Product: Fat burners; Why not: Fat loss is driven by a calorie deficit. If one contains caffeine, you are paying extra for caffeine.. Product: Detox products; Why not: Your liver and kidneys already do this job.. Product: BCAAs and EAAs, if your protein is enough; Why not: Protein already supplies them, and the ISSN suggests whole foods with all essential amino acids.. Product: Glutamine for muscle growth; Why not: No strong reason to expect a benefit if your protein is adequate.. Product: Proprietary blends; Why not: If a blend hides each ingredient's dose, it cannot be checked against evidence.

The label is not a guarantee. Supplements are checked less strictly than medicines. Labels may be inaccurate, and contamination or undeclared ingredients can happen. This Handbook gives no figure for how common this is.. Prefer products with independent third-party testing, where available.. Prefer single ingredients with clear doses over blends.. Be sceptical of promises of fast or dramatic results, and of unofficial sellers.. If you are a tested athlete, use only certified products.

Claim | Standing. Claim: "Supplements build muscle."; Standing: Misleading. Training supplies the signal, and food and sleep support it. Creatine helps the training you can do. It does not replace it.. Claim: "Creatine damages the kidneys."; Standing: Not supported in healthy people. Kidney disease is a separate matter for your doctor.. Claim: "Creatine causes cramps and dehydration."; Standing: Not supported. Athlete studies reported no effect or less of both.. Claim: "You must load creatine."; Standing: False. Loading is faster. A daily dose gets there more slowly.. Claim: "Protein powder is a steroid."; Standing: False. It is concentrated food protein.. Claim: "Natural means safe."; Standing: False. Plant extracts can be active and can interact with medicines.

Energy, protein, sticking with it and sleep come before any supplement.. Creatine monohydrate is the one most worth considering: 3 to 5 g a day, with a strong safety record in healthy people.. Caffeine works best for endurance, and less consistently for strength. Do not trade sleep for it.. Protein powder is convenient food. Compare it with real food on price.. Correct a confirmed deficiency. Do not guess at one.. Blends that hide their doses cannot be judged.

One common claim says drink constantly and hit a fixed daily target. Another says thirst handles everything. The evidence is more contextual. Past a certain point, losing fluid impairs performance. Thirst is a good guide in some conditions and a poor one in others. And drinking too much can be dangerous.

Evidence: moderate. Dehydration of 2% of body mass or more is associated with poorer temperature control, more strain on the heart and, in many conditions, poorer aerobic performance. These conditions include warmer, longer and more intense exercise. In 34 endurance studies with 60 observations, 68% showed significantly impaired performance at this level.. Many of these studies were done in a laboratory, which may not match real conditions.

Two per cent of body mass is 1.4 kg for a 70 kg person. Body mass losses this large take time to build up. This figure concerns aerobic work. It is not established that the same threshold applies to resistance training.

Thirst is a real signal, with a known limit: it tends to ease before you are fully rehydrated. In one study people drinking freely replaced about half of what they lost. When you sweat a lot, that deficit can build up.

Situation | Strategy. Situation: Exercise under about 60 to 90 minutes, in cooler conditions or at lower intensity; Strategy: Drinking to thirst may be enough.. Situation: Exercise over 90 minutes, especially in heat; Strategy: Planned drinking is better.. Situation: Heavy sweating, or sessions where performance matters; Strategy: Planned drinking. Find your sweat rate.. Situation: Indian summer heat, or a gym without air conditioning; Strategy: In practice, treat this like the hot case, however short the session.

Exercise-associated hyponatremia. Drinking far more than your body can get rid of dilutes the sodium in your blood. This is mainly a risk in long endurance events rather than gym training, and it can be life-threatening.. Its symptoms can look like dehydration: headache, nausea, confusion and dizziness. Swollen hands or face are also warning signs. Drinking more can make it worse.. A clear rule: never drink so much that you gain weight during exercise.. Suspected hyponatremia is a medical emergency. Get urgent medical care.
If you train long, hard or in heat, one session can replace a lot of guessing. This is a practical method, and it estimates fluid lost. It does not precisely measure how hydrated you are.

Weigh yourself just before training, in minimal clothing.. Note everything you drink during the session.. Weigh yourself again right after, towelled dry, in the same clothing.. Weight lost plus fluid drunk is roughly your fluid loss. One kilogram is about one litre.
Try it once in cool conditions and once in heat to learn your own range.

Needs vary with your body size, climate, activity and the water in your food, so no single number fits everyone. Levlofit shows a daily water goal, and you can set your own. Treat it as a reminder, not a rule. In practice:

Drink across the day. Tea, coffee, milk, dal and curd count too.. Drink more in heat and around longer or harder sessions.. Start sessions hydrated.. Replace fluid over the hours after a session, not all at once.
Urine colour is a rough check. Pale yellow suggests you are drinking enough, and consistently dark suggests otherwise. Some vitamins and medicines can change it.
Electrolytes are minerals in your body fluids, involved in fluid balance and in nerve and muscle function.

Electrolyte | Why it matters for training. Electrolyte: Sodium; Why it matters for training: The main one lost in sweat, and the one involved in hyponatremia.. Electrolyte: Potassium; Why it matters for training: Lost in smaller amounts. Fruit, vegetables, dal and milk supply it.. Electrolyte: Magnesium, calcium; Why it matters for training: Lost in small amounts. Important in your diet, but rarely a hydration concern.

Cramp. Cramp is often blamed on electrolyte loss or dehydration. A competing view blames nerve and muscle fatigue. This is contested, so do not assume electrolytes will prevent it. Frequent or severe cramps, or cramps at rest, need a clinician.
These are practical suggestions.

Situation | What is enough. Situation: Ordinary gym session in normal conditions; What is enough: Water.. Situation: Long session, heavy sweating or real heat; What is enough: Fluid with some salt. Nimbu paani with salt, or an ORS-style drink, can do this cheaply.. Situation: Endurance exercise over about 90 minutes; What is enough: Fluid, sodium and carbohydrate.. Situation: Trying to lose fat; What is enough: Remember that sports drinks contain calories.
If you have high blood pressure, or kidney or heart disease, ask your doctor about added salt.

Treating a daily target as a requirement. No one number fits everyone.. Assuming thirst is always enough. It becomes less reliable as time, heat and sweat rise.. Assuming more is always safer. Never finish heavier than you started.. Buying sports drinks for a short gym session. Water usually does the job.. Trying to fix hydration during a session. Start hydrated instead.. Blaming every cramp on electrolytes. That can delay finding the real cause.

Dehydration of 2% of body mass or more is linked with poorer aerobic performance.. For shorter, cooler or lighter sessions, drinking to thirst may be enough.. Longer, hotter and harder sessions need planned drinking.. Never gain weight during exercise. Suspected hyponatremia is an emergency.. Sodium is the electrolyte lost most in sweat. The link between cramps and electrolytes is contested.
Restaurants, travel, weddings and festivals are a permanent part of life. A way of eating that only works in your own kitchen will not last.
The ISSN says the long-term success of a diet depends on sticking with it. So how you handle the exceptions matters. The advice below is practical judgement, not research.

Timescale | What it tells you. Timescale: One meal; What it tells you: Very little, against a week or a month.. Timescale: One day; What it tells you: Little on its own.. Timescale: A week; What it tells you: The shortest span worth reacting to.. Timescale: A month or more; What it tells you: Where your body composition really responds.
One large restaurant meal is only a part of a week's food. The bigger cost often comes from your reaction to it.

You may hear that 80% of your meals should be nutritious and 20% flexible. The idea is sound: most of your food should serve your goals, and some can be flexible. The exact ratio is a memory aid, not a finding. Build a week that mostly works, and stop auditing the exceptions.
You are usually choosing from someone else's options, so aim for the best available choice.

What to do | How. What to do: Find the protein; How: Paneer, dal, chana, curd, eggs, chicken, fish or tofu. Restaurant meals often have plenty of energy and less protein.. What to do: Notice the oil; How: Deep-fried dishes and rich gravies usually have far more calories than tandoori, grilled, roasted or dry versions.. What to do: Count your drinks; How: Sugary drinks, juice and alcohol add calories with little fullness.. What to do: Watch portions; How: Sharing, or stopping when comfortable, often works better than deciding beforehand to eat half.. What to do: Add volume; How: A salad, raita or vegetable side can replace some richer food.
Do not arrive starving. Skipping meals to "save" calories for an event can backfire and lead to eating more. Eat normally through the day, with protein, then enjoy the event.

It contains calories, without much fullness, so they are easy to miss.. Mixers add more, especially soft drinks and juices.. It can disturb your sleep, even if it makes you drowsy.. It can loosen your food decisions during and after drinking.
Levlofit makes no health recommendation about drinking. That is a personal and medical matter. If your progress has stalled and alcohol is regular, count it before you decide your plan has failed.

Carry protein. Roasted chana, peanuts, whey in a shaker, or milk cartons where available.. Carry water. Travel days make it easy to drink too little.. Do not skip meals because the options are imperfect. An imperfect meal usually beats a missed one.. Expect your weight to move for reasons other than fat. Salt, fluid, fibre and timing all change. Your seven-day average will smooth this out.. Walk. Travel is otherwise very still.
A missed week of training does not undo months of work. The bigger risk is returning at your old loads straight away, so ease back in.
Indian festival seasons can be long and full of food. Treating each one as a threat is miserable and unnecessary.

Eat normally, with protein, during the day.. Eat what you want at the occasion.. Return to your usual pattern at the next meal, not next Monday.. Do not punish yourself with extra exercise or restriction afterwards.

Compensation is the pattern to watch. Skipping meals before an event, exercising to "cancel" food, restricting hard the next day, or feeling a lot of guilt about a meal can turn an ordinary occasion into a problem.. These can also be early signs of a difficult relationship with food. If the pattern continues, feels hard to control or affects your daily life, talk to a qualified clinician or dietitian. This Handbook does not diagnose or treat eating disorders.
Hostel mess, conference food, long journeys, family obligations. In order of usefulness:
