Recovery shows what sleep loss costs you. This chapter looks the other way: how much sleep is recommended, what happens when you sleep more on purpose, and which familiar sleep advice has evidence behind it.
Evidence: strong, by consensus. A joint statement from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society supports 7 or more hours a night, regularly, for adults aged 18 to 60.
Notice that this is a floor, not a range. Seven hours is the minimum to aim for. If you often wake unrested after seven, try more.

Evidence: moderate, from limited studies. A review of 25 sleep intervention studies in athletes found that sleeping longer at night and napping were the most effective of the methods tested for improving performance. The authors acknowledge the limited amount of high-quality evidence.
You cannot decide to fall asleep. You can decide to be in bed earlier. If you are often short of sleep, this is likely to be the most useful change in this chapter.

The standard advice has thin support in athletes. The same review found sleep hygiene advice and removing electronic devices at night had no effect on sleep and later performance. These results come from only a few studies.
So:

Do not stop these habits if they help you. They are free, and a few studies do not prove they never work.. Do not expect much from them alone. If your sleep is truly poor, a neater bedtime routine may not be the fix.. Put your effort into time in bed. That has better support.

Habit | Standing. Habit: Enough time in bed; Standing: Has the better support.. Habit: Steady wake time, including weekends; Standing: Common advice, low cost.. Habit: Dark, cool, quiet room; Standing: Common advice, low cost.. Habit: Limiting late caffeine; Standing: Sensible. Caffeine can affect sleep, and this varies between people.. Habit: Fewer screens before bed; Standing: Removing devices showed no effect in a few athlete studies. Keep it if it helps you.. Habit: Alcohol before bed; Standing: It can make you drowsy and still disturb your sleep.

The same review found naps among the most effective methods overall. A nap is a reasonable option if you are short of sleep. It does not replace your night's sleep. Keep it early enough that it does not push back your bedtime, and if you nap before a session, notice whether you actually perform better.

You will often hear that poor sleep causes injury. A review of 12 cohort studies concluded that current evidence does not support poor sleep as an independent risk factor for injury in adult athletes, and that the studies were too mixed to settle the question.
The case for sleep rests on performance, and that is strong enough.

In a large review, sleep loss lowered exercise performance by about 7.6% on average. Afternoon and evening sessions consistently suffered, while morning sessions were largely unaffected. If a bad night is unavoidable and your session cannot move, train earlier if you can.

The consensus recommendation is for regular sleep. It is not established that weekend catch-up fully reverses a week of short nights. Treat extra sleep as useful and partial: better than nothing, and worse than not building the debt.

See a clinician. If your sleep stays bad, more routine tips may not be the answer, and looking for them may delay real help. See a qualified clinician if you have:. Trouble falling or staying asleep over several weeks, despite enough time in bed.. Loud snoring, pauses in breathing, gasping or choking in your sleep, or waking unrefreshed after long sleep.. Overwhelming daytime sleepiness, or falling asleep without meaning to.. Sleep problems alongside lasting low mood, anxiety or loss of interest.. Restless, uncomfortable feelings in your legs at night.. Insomnia and other sleep disorders are medical conditions with treatments. Levlofit does not diagnose them or recommend sleep medicine.

Treating seven hours as the whole target. The statement says 7 or more.. Perfecting the routine instead of the duration. Time in bed has better support.. Expecting routine changes to fix real insomnia. If they have not worked in a few weeks, see a clinician.. Napping into the evening. It can eat into your night's sleep.. Using injury claims as motivation. The performance case is real without them.

Aim for 7 or more hours a night, regularly.. Spending longer in bed is the change with the better support.. Naps can help. They do not replace your night's sleep.. Sleep hygiene and removing devices showed no effect in a few athlete studies.. It is not established that poor sleep alone causes injury.. Sleep problems that last deserve a clinician.
Stress is usually described as something that slows your recovery. The better-supported effect is simpler: stress makes you less likely to train at all. That changes what you should do about it.

Evidence: moderate to strong for the effect on behaviour. Of 55 prospective studies, 76.4% found that psychological stress predicted less physical activity or more sitting. Among higher-quality studies, it was 85.7%.. Some studies, 18.2%, found the opposite, with stress leading to more exercise. The authors note that habitually active people exercise more under stress, while those just starting exercise less.
The most useful point in this chapter. The habit itself can protect you. The early work of making training automatic may be what keeps you going through stressful periods later.

It is not established here that stress directly slows your physical recovery between sessions. It is plausible, and stress can disturb your sleep, which does affect performance. None of the advice below depends on that claim.

Exercise may also help how you feel. A large review of trials found walking, jogging, yoga and strength training eased depression, with effects that seemed comparable to some established treatments, though with less confidence in the evidence. That is useful. It does not make training a replacement for care. For stress specifically, the review above found only early evidence that stress management combined with exercise protects activity levels.

Area: Sleep; What happens: Harder to fall or stay asleep.; Standing: Practical observation. Sleep loss then affects performance.. Area: Eating; What happens: Eating much more or less, and less regularly.; Standing: Practical observation.. Area: Effort; What happens: You attend, but train less hard.; Standing: Practical observation.

In most prospective studies, stress predicted less activity.. People just starting tend to lose sessions to stress. Habitually active people often train more.. Warm-up and mobility covers what stretching does. This chapter asks the practical question: if you already lift, how much separate mobility work do you need? Often less than you might think.

Term | Meaning. Term: Mobility; Meaning: The range you can reach and control at a joint. It needs strength through that range.. Term: Flexibility; Meaning: The range available at a joint, usually measured passively.
Stretching does not make muscles longer. Fascicle length did not change after one session or many. Stiffness fell, and with repeated stretching, tolerance to the stretch rose.

Evidence: moderate. A review of 55 studies found that resistance training increased range of motion (effect size 0.73). It showed no significant difference from stretching (0.08, p = 0.79). Combining the two did no better than stretching alone (-0.001, p = 0.99). The authors conclude that stretching before or after resistance training may not be necessary to improve flexibility.. Untrained and sedentary people gained more (1.042) than trained or active people (0.43). Using only body mass did not significantly improve range.

What this means for you. If you train with external load through a full range, a separate stretching routine may add little. Full range on your working sets can also be part of your mobility work, so cutting depth to add load costs you twice.

A position you cannot reach limits an exercise you want, such as squat depth or a comfortable overhead position.. You cannot yet load the range at all. You may need to open it first.. You train only with bodyweight. The result above may not apply to you.. You want range for something outside lifting. A sport, an activity or comfort. That is a fair personal reason.
Otherwise, a general daily stretching routine is a habit you may enjoy, not something you need.

Approach | Effect on jumping and sprinting. Approach: Dynamic alone; Effect on jumping and sprinting: Improved jump height and sprint time.. Approach: Static, then dynamic; Effect on jumping and sprinting: Improved jump height.. Approach: Static alone, just before; Effect on jumping and sprinting: Made sprint time worse.
These studies measured explosive tasks, so the effect on an ordinary set may differ.
In practice: if a static stretch helps you reach a position, use it, then do dynamic movement and warm-up sets. Without such a limit, skip it.

Area: Ankles; What it can limit: Squat depth and knee path; Standing: Not established that ankle drills change results. Test your own depth.. Area: Shoulders and upper back; What it can limit: Overhead positions, pressing setup; Standing: Mechanically clear. Specific drills are not tested here.. Area: Hamstrings; What it can limit: Hip hinge depth; Standing: Often stiffness and tolerance. Loaded hinging through a full range is a good place to start.

Pick a routine you will keep up. One review found hold time and frequency played little role in how much range people gained.. Load the range you gain, so you can use it.. Target the real limit. A muscle can feel tight without being what limits you.. Expect months. A warm-up uses range you already have.
Here is a practical example, if your squat depth is limited and nothing hurts:

Step | What to do. Step: Test; What to do: Film your depth from the side, with the camera in the same place each time.. Step: Load what you have; What to do: Squat under load to your full available depth, every session.. Step: Add targeted work if needed; What to do: Add ankle and hip work before the session if it lets you reach further that day.. Step: Retest; What to do: After six to eight weeks, not weekly.
If your depth has not moved after a couple of months, ask a qualified professional whether something structural is limiting you.

Mobility and injury. It is not established that mobility work prevents injury. The stronger evidence for lower injury risk is strength training itself, in sports groups. Train mobility because it lets you do exercises you otherwise could not.

Doing a general daily routine and expecting more range. If you already lift through a full range, it may add little.. Cutting range on working sets, then stretching to fix it. Your working sets could be doing that job.. Stretching whatever feels tight. Tightness is a feeling, not a diagnosis.. Testing weekly. Change takes months.. Expecting a warm-up to build range. It uses what you have.. Forcing a painful position. Stop instead.

Resistance training with load improved range of motion about as well as stretching.. Full range on your working sets helps your mobility.. Stretching lowers stiffness and raises tolerance. It does not lengthen muscle.. Dedicated work suits a specific limit, bodyweight-only training or goals outside lifting.. Avoid static stretching alone right before explosive work.. Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is the ache that appears a day or two after unfamiliar or hard exercise. The review below describes it as coming from intense, unaccustomed exercise. It tells you less about your training than many people assume.
This chapter separates three questions: what soreness is, what reduces it, and whether reducing it does anything for your training.

Soreness usually peaks a day or two after a session, and it is most likely after unfamiliar work: a new plan, a return after a break, a new exercise or a jump in volume. Its exact cause is not settled, and nothing practical here depends on settling it.

Repeat the same session a week or two later and you will usually be less sore, even with the same or more work. So soreness mostly tells you the work was unfamiliar. It does not tell you the work was productive.

In practice. A productive session after months of training may leave you barely sore. A new session can leave you very sore and still give you little. Chasing soreness adds recovery cost. Judge your sessions by your logged performance over weeks.
There is also evidence behind this. In one small study, muscle damage peaked early in training and was not related to later growth.

Evidence: moderate for direction, with a serious quality warning. A review of 29 systematic reviews, covering 863 trials and 24 treatments, reported effects on soreness at various time points from cooling therapy, cryostimulation, contrast therapy, massage, phototherapy and kinesiotaping. Evidence for stretching, exercise and electrical stimulation was weak.. Seventeen of the 29 reviews were of critically low quality, and only two were high quality. The authors say the evidence has uncertainties and weaknesses.

Less pain is not the same as better results. These findings are about soreness, a feeling. They do not show that a treatment speeds up your performance recovery or improves your results. Feeling better is a fair goal. It is just a different goal.
Probably the most practical way to limit soreness is not on those lists: progress gradually, so the work is rarely unfamiliar.

Common advice: Electrical stimulation; Standing: Weak evidence overall.. Common advice: Warming up to prevent it; Standing: Not established.. Common advice: Extra protein to prevent it; Standing: Not established. Protein matters for other reasons.

Situation: Severe soreness limiting normal movement; Reasonable response: Train something else or cut back a lot. Then ask whether your volume rose too quickly.. It means knowing the one picture that needs immediate attention.

Reducing is reasonable. You rarely need to stop.. Testing sore muscles with heavy loads. That is a poor day to find out.. Raising volume so quickly you are badly sore again and again. Slow down.

Recovery tools are sold on a promise: use them and you will adapt faster. Several have evidence for making you less sore, which is a smaller claim. And one popular tool has evidence of harming the strength gains you train for, so it comes first.

Evidence: moderate, and negative for strength. A review of eight articles on regular cold-water immersion, at 15 °C or below, alongside training found a harmful effect on one-repetition maximum, maximum isometric strength and strength endurance (effect size -0.60, -0.87 to -0.33). It did not appear to affect aerobic performance.

What this means for you. If you lift to get stronger, do not make cold-water immersion after sessions a routine habit. You may be trading less soreness for smaller strength gains.. It may be a fair trade when you must perform again soon, such as during a tournament. Treat that as a deliberate choice, not a default.
A quick cold shower because you like it is not what was studied.

Question | What the evidence says. Question: Does it reduce soreness?; What the evidence says: For several tools, yes, from a large but weak literature.. Question: Does it speed up performance recovery?; What the evidence says: Not established here for these tools.. Question: Does it improve your training results?; What the evidence says: No tool here has shown this. Regular cold-water immersion had a harmful effect on strength.

Motivation is often discussed and rarely measured. One part has been studied: why some reasons for training last while others fade. Much of the rest is sensible practice without strong evidence, and this chapter labels it that way.
It also draws an important line between low motivation, which can be a training problem, and low mood, which is not.
Motivation is often set against discipline. Research on this has looked at something else: whether your reasons come from you, or feel pushed on you.

Evidence: moderate. A review of 66 studies found consistent support for a link between more autonomous motivation and exercise. Valuing the outcome tended to predict starting more strongly, while enjoying or finding the activity itself worthwhile better predicted long-term exercise.. Feeling competent and having more intrinsic motives also predicted exercise across many groups.. Most of the studies were non-experimental, so this shows association, not proven cause.
So the question is not only whether you can summon willpower on a bad day. It is whether your reason for training tends to last through bad days.
Wanting to look different is a fair reason to start. The same review found mixed evidence for body-related motives as a predictor of exercise.
What to do with that. Keep your physique goal. Add a second reason that does not depend on the mirror: getting stronger at something specific, enjoying your session, or improving a skill.
Not wanting to train can sometimes be information about your plan. Before treating it as a character flaw, check these:

Check | Why. Check: Sleep; Why: Sleep loss lowers physical performance.. Check: Life stress; Why: Stress predicted less activity in most prospective studies.. Check: Training volume; Why: More is not always better, and recovery has a cost.. Check: Food; Why: Too little food can leave you flat.
Dread and flatness are not proven measures of training stress. Treat them as a prompt to check the list above. Your logged performance over weeks is a better guide.

Signs that need a clinician, not a lighter week. Low mood or loss of interest most of the day, most days, for two weeks or more, including things you normally enjoy.. Sleep or appetite changes that do not follow your training.. Training that feels compulsive: distress at missing a session, training through injury or illness, or sessions pushing out work, study or relationships.. Food rules narrowing, or guilt and compensation after eating.. Constant worry about not being muscular enough, whatever your mirror or log shows.. Using alcohol or other substances to manage how you feel.. Thoughts of harming yourself. In India, call Tele-MANAS on 14416 at any time, or your local emergency services.. None of this means you failed at discipline. These are reasons to talk to a qualified clinician, and a handbook cannot assess you.
Exercise may help your mood, and trials suggest it can ease depression. That is not a reason to manage these signs alone.

A lighter week when training feels heavy is reasonable and common. The guidance comes from expert agreement, not experiments. So it is a fair choice, not a requirement. Sometimes the honest reason is that you would rather train next month than grind through this one.
These cost nothing and many people like them. Take what helps and ignore the rest.

Evidence: no consensus on cause. A review of 41 systematic reviews looked at spine posture, physical activity and low back pain. They reported both positive and null associations for spine posture, prolonged standing, sitting, bending and twisting, awkward postures and heavy physical work.. Its conclusion: "Despite the availability of many reviews, there is no consensus regarding causality of physical exposure to LBP. Association has been documented but does not provide a causal explanation for LBP."
This does not say posture never matters, and it is no recommendation to slouch. It says the confident story, where bad posture causes your pain and fixing it cures your pain, is not established.

Evidence: association in adults, not established as cause. A review of 15 cross-sectional studies found adults with neck pain had more forward head posture than those without. In adolescents there was no significant difference. Age played an important role.. All the studies were cross-sectional, which means they measured people at one point in time, so this design cannot show which came first.

The missing link in adolescents is interesting. If this posture simply caused neck pain, you might expect the link at all ages. It might instead reflect age, or people in pain holding themselves differently. That is reasoning, not a finding.

Body weight is the cheapest measurement in this Handbook, and among the most misread. A decent scale has little error, while your body's daily changes are large. That combination decides everything below.
Use a seven-day average. Judge your weight by a seven-day average, not one reading. Weigh most days in the same conditions, average the last seven readings, and compare that average week to week.
Averaging works because daily swings partly cancel out. Your body does not change when you take an average. Your measurement improves.
A rolling average also updates every day, so one missed weigh-in does little harm.

Evidence: moderate. In ten studies of habit programmes for physical activity, problem solving was linked with better results (0.36, 0.17 to 0.55), and action planning was among the common techniques. The overall effect was small to medium (0.31, 0.14 to 0.48).

Evidence: moderate, from two more sources. Whose goal it is matters. A review of 66 studies found consistent support for a link between more autonomous motivation and exercise.. Choosing your own helps. In a review of 20 studies, self-selected habits generally gave stronger habits.

Many people stop training. What distinguishes those who do not? The evidence has a partial answer, and it does not come down to willpower.

Evidence: moderate. A review of 66 studies found consistent support for a link between more autonomous motivation and exercise. Valuing the outcome tended to predict starting, while intrinsic motivation better predicted long-term exercise. Feeling competent also predicted exercise. Most studies were non-experimental, so this shows association, not proven cause.
In practice, the reason that gets you started may not be the one that keeps you going. It helps if training becomes something you would do anyway.
Median time to form a habit was 59 to 66 days, and individuals ranged from 4 to 335 days. Someone at the far end took most of a year and was not doing anything wrong.

Stress predicted less physical activity in 76.4% of 55 prospective studies. Some found the opposite, with habitually active people exercising more under stress. So the years you have already put in may help protect you.

Missing one opportunity did not materially affect habit formation in one well-known study. "Never miss twice" is a catchy saying, not a finding. Keep it if it helps, but do not treat a second miss as failure.

Few people train only one thing forever. A runner may want strength, and a lifter may want better fitness. The old fear was that mixing strength and cardio would blunt the results of both. The current evidence is more specific, and kinder.

Evidence: strong. A review of 43 studies compared combined aerobic and strength training with strength training alone. It found no meaningful loss in maximal strength (effect size -0.06, -0.20 to 0.09) or muscle growth (-0.01, -0.16 to 0.18).. The gain that did suffer was explosive strength (-0.28, -0.48 to -0.08), more so when both were done in the same session than when sessions were at least 3 hours apart.
So strength and muscle gains generally hold up. If explosive work matters to you, keep it apart from cardio when you can.

This is practical guidance. Choose one main goal, and let it have first claim on your training days. Add other kinds of training at a smaller, steady dose. If you run out of days, trim the smaller dose first. Levlofit lets you rank your goals, and your plan shows you how they fit your week.

Evidence: uncertain, from one exploratory study. A one-year study followed 874 novice runners. Overall, injury rates did not differ significantly between those increasing weekly distance by under 10%, 10 to 30%, or over 30%.. For distance-related injuries specifically, those increasing by more than 30% had a higher rate than those under 10% (hazard ratio 1.59), but the interval included no effect (0.96 to 2.66). The authors suggest novices may be well advised to stay under 30% a week.

So no percentage is proven safe, including the popular "10% rule". A sensible approach is to change one thing at a time: distance, number of sessions or intensity. Pain that continues or gets worse is a reason to stop and get it checked.

Stop when quality drops. If a hard session has fallen well below your intended pace, you are training a slower pace while tired. End it early. Stop right away if you feel chest pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness.

Athletic training here means power: moving your own body quickly and forcefully. It is usually trained early in a session, before anything that would tire you.

Evidence: strong. A meta-analysis of 56 studies on jump training found the largest gains in jump height came from programmes longer than 10 weeks, with more than 20 sessions, and with more than 50 jumps a session. Combining jump types beat using only one. Adding weight gave no extra benefit.
Those are amounts for maximising jump height, not a starting point. If you are new to jumping, start with far less, and build up.
It makes practical sense to do this work fresh, since the quality of each jump matters.
